speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: MCINTYRE PORCUPINE MINES
subtopic: QUESTION AS TO REJECTION OF CONCILIATION BOARD RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Labour. Has the minister received notification that McIntyre Porcupine Mines Limited has rejected the recommendations of the board of conciliation appointed by the government, recommendations which had been accepted by local 100 of the Porcupine Mine Workers Union, and that a decision to strike has been taken? In view of the substantial assistance, amounting to $22 million, given to this company under the Emergency 55946-2434
Gold Mining Assistance Act, will the government take all steps necessary in the public interest to persuade the company to accept the conciliation board's recommendations, and thus bring the dispute to an end?

maintopic: MCINTYRE PORCUPINE MINES
subtopic: QUESTION AS TO REJECTION OF CONCILIATION BOARD RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
My hon. friend no doubt knows that this dispute comes under provincial jurisdiction. I believe the majority report recommended an increase in pay, certain paid holidays, and some form of check-off. I have no jurisdiction. Under legislation in force now, neither the federal government nor the provinces can enforce the findings of a conciliation board. I have always held the opinion that the sun does not shine on only one side of the fence. I know that employees sometimes turn down the majority report of the board. I take the long view that both industry and labour would be well advised to accept the majority report of a conciliation board.
At the moment there are some major disputes under my jurisdiction in which the majority report of the board has been turned down by the employees. I am fearful that the whole system of conciliation could easily break down if some judgment is not used by both sides in connection with the machinery that has been built up over the years, whether it be provincial or federal.

speechtext:
Perhaps my hon. friend will permit me to make an explanation in his

favour, and also a correction, or perhaps I should say a clarification. Last evening, speaking of unemployment figures, the hon. member for Cape Breton South mentioned 57,000, which I mistakenly understood to refer to Nova Scotia. Later I said the figure for Nova Scotia was 13,000, which was correct as of June 8. In reviewing Hansard this morning at page 3826 I discovered that my hon. friend was referring to the maritime provinces, which until recently we have considered as including Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. The total number of unemployed for those three provinces as of June 8, 1950, was 30,100. In addition there were 19,600 in Newfoundland as of that date. The total for Canada as of June 8. 1950 was 239,800, which is a drop of 193,000 from the peak which occurred last March. That is satisfactory, I hope.

maintopic: FLOOD CONDITIONS
subtopic: FRASER RIVER VALLEY-INQUIRY AS TO PRESENT SITUATION
speechtext:
That is the very point I rose to bring to the minister's attention. My quarrel with the Department of Labour in listing the unemployed is that the figures now mentioned by the minister should have been given to hon. members at intervals of at least two weeks. That was done in the past; every two weeks the department would issue a statement on the unemployment situation in Canada. Those releases went to the two congresses of labour and to the press, as well as certain members of the house who were on the mailing list. That practice has been discontinued.
Last evening, when hon. members rose to discuss the unemployment situation, the only figures they had to work on were those issued about a month ago. I believe those figures came out about June 3, and gave the position as of about May 18. At that time the national picture as set out by the department showed some 306,000 unemployed. The figure for the maritimes was 41,000. Since then there has been a considerable drop, and personally I think it is unfair for the department to issue figures arid then, when there has been a substantial change in the right direction, to leave hon. members with figures a month old while the minister can rise in his place and fire back figures which are much later, and which we do not know about.
Recently there has been a great deal of controversy between the congress of labour and the department over the withholding of the actual unemployment situation as it is reported by the various offices across the country. I do not think the department is being smart in this. If there is a change in the right direction I believe the smart thing for the department to do is at least to keep the

congresses of labour and the members of this house advised of the changes that take place from time to time.
The figures just given by the minister show a substantial decrease in unemployment. Before the estimates are through I hope the minister will be able to give us, province by province, the job opportunities that were created and that brought about this drop of some 198,000 since the last release. This morning I happened to pick up a press release from the office in Glace Bay, my home town, and there has not been very much of a change there. This press clipping is dated June 16, and it states:
Unemployment figures released today by the local office of the national employment service show a slight drop over last week's total.
This week there are 129 females and 432 males listed as unemployed as against the 130 females and 467 males registered last week, a decline of 35 . . .
The important part of this is that 279 men and 68 women are claiming benefits through the local employment office.
The point I want to make for the minister's benefit, as I argued last night, is that special unemployment relief, or an extension of the supplementary benefits, should be given to those areas. This press release from the local employment office in that particular town shows that over fifty per cent of the total unemployed registered in that town are not receiving unemployment insurance. That is another indication of what I stated last night, namely, that the unemployment problem in the maritimes is largely a permanent one. It is a problem that the municipal authorities, who now have the responsibility of looking after the totally unemployed, are not able to handle.
I am suggesting that instead of accepting unemployment as it is on a national scale and deciding that it is seasonal and regional, the fair thing to do across Canada would be to make a regional survey, particularly in the maritimes, to ascertain the amount of permanent unemployment there. In that way you will get a fair picture of what is necessary in that part of the country, because this press release definitely shows that there is a permanent unemployment problem in the maritimes. I know that most of the towns and cities in the maritimes have such a heavy municipal burden that they are not in a position to carry unemployment relief. There is an act on the statute book, known as the Unemployment Relief and Assistance Act, which provides that when a certain percentage of a municipality, town or city is totally unemployed the act can be applied through the provincial government.
Supply-Labour
Something of that kind is necessary in some of the towns and cities in the maritime provinces.
What I really want to say is that if unemployment is declining in Canada we are glad to hear it. In future I would like the minister at least to keep hon. members informed as to that decline. We do not want to rise in our places in this house and misrepresent the picture. All we can do is to take the figures that are released publicly from time to time and make an analysis of them. From now on I should like to get the figures that the department has compiled.

Let me make this 'clear. As long as I am the Minister of Labour, I will run my department. So far as I am concerned, let the sun shine in. I am one of the few people who never closes his office door. My door is always open, except when someone is in there talking to me. No official in my department is going to tell me what to do. They have said to me at times: "If I were you I would do this." But I have said: "You are not me; to be me you have to be elected" and that is not the easiest thing in the world.
My hon. friend can rest assured that these figures are in the Labour Gazette. They have been criticized as being handouts by departments. Let me be frank. Any member of this house, irrespective of what side he sits on, if he wants the information and asks me for it, he will get it. I have always maintained, as my hon. friend knows, that you cannot face a problem by running away from it.
As I said last night, it is sometimes not the wisest thing to do to quote figures from memory, especially in relation to a large department like the Department of Labour. I should like to impress upon my hon. friend the fact that employment is a dynamic thing; it is not static. There are changes from day to day; different people come and go, and so forth.
As I pointed out last night, 1,700,000 people passed through the employment service alone last year. Along with my hon. friend and other hon. members, I take pride in the efficiency of the labour department. I have been very fortunate in building that organization, to have a group of loyal civil servants-* exceptionally loyal, may I say.
I agree with my hon. friend that anything we can possibly do to meet the problems of my department will be done by my officials and myself. If he ever wants any information- it does not matter how uncomfortable it is

* from me, I will give it to him.

In order to speak on this subject we have to understand both sides. Any man taking part in debate who knows only one side is pretty sure of defeat. I think I know labour from all points of view: first from the point of view of the man who toils, and afterwards from the point of view of one who had the opportunity and responsibility of hiring labour. I know it from the contractor's point of view, too. I have found there are four types of people who have their rights. The man who puts up the money for an industry has his rights, whether that industry is a wholesale or a retail concern, a coal mine or a pipe line. The management of industry have their rights. They have the right to be protected. The workers, too, have their rights. I admit that I am a good deal biased toward the man who toils. Then the consumers have their rights.

We have to see this question of labour from all angles. My first word is that the former prime minister certainly understood labour and industry, as he wrote and as he practised it afterwards; otherwise he would not have put the name of Tom Moore, the former president of the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, on the honour list of the king. No doubt his advice was that Tom Moore should receive the Order of the British Empire. I dare not say, Mr. Chairman, that there are others who should be in that honour list. I say my word now for the present Minister of Labour. He is not a graduate of a university; he is a graduate of labour. Had he been a graduate of a university he would not have said, as he did a moment ago, that the sun does not always shine on the one side of the fence. Had he graduated from a university he would have said that the sun shines down in all its majesty over all classes and distinctions of men, irrespective of class or creed. Which is the plainer?
In 1941 I sat over there and watched the proceedings. If the Department of Labour was ever in a mess, it was then. We had a labour board. Applications were piled high. The board was made up of experts, but they did not have the ability to handle their work quickly enough to keep the department out of trouble. Then our former prime minister came along and appointed the present Minister of Labour to the post he now holds. I met him first in Fort William, when we had difficulty in connection with unemployed as related to the relief camps. I cannot forget his statement to me then, that when a man does a day's work he should have a day's pay. He also said that if a man gets a day's pay he should do a day's work. That is what the minister has been saying ever since.
What happened? That labour board was changed. The deputy minister was appointed, and since then I do not think one would find a labour department in any country in the world that has done better work than the department presided over by the present minister. He showed good judgment when he did not allow his deputy minister to go. He gave him another year; and I hope he will give him another, and another and another, so that there will not be any loss to the country.
We have in Fort William business concerns paying salaries to their employees. In addition they pay commissions. Perhaps the hon. member for Calgary East would refer to that as profit sharing, but when a man goes into one of those stores he gets service and gets it immediately. I have gone into large places of business here in Ottawa-that is, large for

this city-and I have waited five or ten minutes before being served. The other day I could not wait any longer and had to go without being served. If those clerks were working on commission there would be a different story, because they would be anxious to earn their commissions.
I agree with those who have spoken that labour should have a share in profits. It would put pep into labourers, and it would be a good move for industry. The minister has said that a well-run labour union is a great asset to labour and to industry. We have that condition in Fort William, and, as has been happening in other places, we have been getting rid of the troublesome element. But a union run by someone who is narrow or selfish is a curse to labour, and such a leader does not earn his money. What we need is to have labour and management working together and, as the minister said, putting their feet under the table and talking across to each other on a fifty-fifty basis. When we have that we shall be making progress.
As another hon. member has pointed out, we have unemployment insurance and family allowances, both of which have helped us at the lakehead during our seasonal unemployment. That is one thing that stands out. I admired very much the way in which the national registration was carried out across this country. It was a difficult job, but they knew where the workers were, and whether or not they were working. I have taken, this opportunity this morning to pay my tribute to the minister and to make the request that when the next king's honour list is brought out, consideration be given to him and his administration of the department.

Recently a case was brought to my attention which I think should receive the consideration of the minister and his staff. An application was made for an annuity by a husband and wife, the husband then being in poor health. Practically all their savings were put into a joint survivor annuity. The husband died shortly after, and within a year the wife died also leaving a son about twelve years of age. Legally the position is that nothing can be paid to that boy.
I believe the amount paid in was $22,108, and $3,500 was received by the wife before her death, leaving a difference of $18,608. The present position is that a married daughter must provide for this young boy. I realize that legally nothing can be done in a case of this kind, but I suggest that the department take some steps to help out in this case. I suggest also that the annuities officers across the country be warned to look into each application to determine whether children are involved. I cannot believe that this father and mother would have taken out this contract if they had realized that nothing would be left for the small boy.
As I say, the father was in poor health at the time the application was made. The married daughter says that her father and mother believed that provision was being made for the mother and for the boy. A warning should be placed on the application forms to indicate that children will not be protected by that type of contract. I understand that until 1945 it was possible to buy a contract with a guarantee that would provide for a certain number of annual payments even if the applicants died before they were completed, but for some reason that contract was discontinued.
I ask the minister to see if something cannot be done for this unfortunate lad, and I wish he would review the possibility of taking some steps to prevent a recurrence of a case of this kind. I think it could be done by giving adequate warning to applicants for annuities that their children will not be protected by a contract of this kind.

Of the 158,959 employees included up to March 31, 1950. 36,973 were no longer participating for reason of retirement, death or termination of service, leaving a net total of 121,986 active participants.
In addition to group annuity contracts, approximately 300 pension plans covering about 8,000 employees were underwritten by individual contracts.

Retirement annuity plans are underwritten by entering into a group annuity contract where a large number of employees is involved, and individual contracts for the smaller organizations. The premium rates are the same in each method of underwriting and are similar to the rates applicable to persons purchasing annuities as individuals. The normal type of plan is contributory, the employee paying a fixed percentage of earnings and the employer paying a similar amount or such amount as may be necessary to complete the purchase of a fixed annuity. The employer generally makes additional payments in respect of prior services. When an employee's service is terminated prior to retirement, he cannot withdraw his money but is credited with a paid-up annuity purchased by his own contributions and such part of the employer contributions as the contract may prescribe. In the event of his death before retirement, the total of his own contributions with interest and such part of the company contributions as the contract may prescribe will be paid to his heirs. On retirement, the annuity purchased by all contributions made on his behalf will be paid to him for life and generally carrying a guarantee that payments will be made for a minimum of five years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The administration item of the Department of National Health and Welfare provides the one opportunity during a session of parliament when the matter of the health of the people of Canada may be discussed. I have always felt that we devoted altogether too little time to the discussion of this important matter.
In previous debates in other sessions I have quoted statistics showing the health situation in this country, and those statistics have invariably indicated that while much has been accomplished in the way of prevention, cure and treatment in certain diseases, there is still a great work to be done. We still have diseases, such as cancer, which offer a challenge to all who are interested in the health of our people, "specially to those engaged in research. It
(Mr. Bater.]
is apparent that if research is to provide the answer to these questions, this house must consider the advisability of voting sums of money for that work.
When the estimates of this department were before the committee last session I drew attention to the fact that conditions were changing with respect to the types of diseases now being treated by physicians and encountered in hospitals. We have made marked progress in the protection of our population against communicable diseases. The advent of penicillin and the sulpha drugs has changed the whole picture in the treatment of infection. Maternal and infant mortality have fallen, and the span of life has been greatly lengthened by these new discoveries. It is true that we have not discovered how to treat and cure such diseases as cancer, disseminated sclerosis, leukemia or poliomyelitis, commonly known as infantile paralysis; and these are only a few of the great problems facing us at the present time. Though tuberculosis is still a menace, modern treatment and care have markedly reduced the incidence of that disease, and I think we can look forward with confidence to the time when it will be entirely eliminated. This may sound optimistic, but we have only to look at the reduced incidence of infections to see that this will be possible in the future.

While new scientific discoveries have been made and will be made, our policy should be directed toward making available to all our people the opportunity for treatment, and bringing to them all the advantages of new scientific discoveries to combat disease and misery. We must constantly strive to bring the standard of health of the people of Canada to the highest possible level. But in making progress in lengthening the span of life we must be prepared to deal with diseases of advancing age. Some of the results of the increase in the number of older people are now becoming apparent. During the last year there has been an increase in the number of mental cases; in fact, as I have said during the last two or three sessions of the house, the percentage of people suffering mental disease is greater than the percentage increase in our general population. Increasing the span of life is going to increase the percentage of people suffering from the mental disturbances which occur in aged people; and unless we find an answer to the problem of cancer it is to be expected that this disease will increase among the older group.
Heart disease is becoming more common, not only from the strain and stress of our modern life but from the increase in the number of older people. Our population is increasing; our towns and cities are growing with the establishment of industries. We must be prepared to deal with an increasing number of health and accident problems connected with our industries. As an example of these changed conditions, though it does not enter into what we are discussing today, we have only to look at the toll of accidents and injuries on our highways. So we must readjust our present and future health facilities to take care of the older age groups. This is going to entail provision for people suffering from mental diseases of the aged, and the treatment of chronic diseases of old people.
I again call attention, Mr. Chairman, to the necessity for research into the cause, prevention and treatment of the so-called degenerative diseases. It is important that the rising mortality rate in heart disease should receive attention. Coronary disease of the heart was formerly regarded as a disease of the older age groups, but it is becoming increasingly common in younger groups. The study of cardiovascular disease, in view of the high casualty rate, should receive the attention of our research workers, in order that the rapidly rising mortality rate may be cut down.
The programs of prevention of acute and communicable diseases carried on by the
Supply-Health and Welfare health departments of all the provinces have shown splendid results. This has been proved by the decreasing mortality rates. One might take as an example the lowered rate of infantile mortality. Preventive treatment has cut down the incidence and costs to the nation of acute diseases. The same form of program can also be highly effective in the control and prevention of chronic diseases, and this is a program which will be increasingly necessary in the future. Not only must we continue our program of prevention; we must pay particular attention to the education of our people in preventive measures. Further, the increase in the span of life makes it absolutely necessary that, along with other measures, old age pensions and assistance to the aged should be commensurate with a decent standard of living for our aged citizens, and any plans for the future must recognize this fact. I am not bringing into this debate the matter that is now before a committee of this house, but I am throwing out the suggestion that it is part of any medical program dealing with the diseases of our elderly citizens.
It is worthy of note that the percentage of venereal disease in Canada shows a marked decline. I was interested in the remarks of Dr. Theodore Rosenthal, director of the New York city bureau of adult hygiene, at the meeting of the Canadian and Ontario public health associations. Among other things Dr. Rosenthal stated that the social aspect, through better family relations, was important. He further said that public education has gone a long way toward bringing about the incidence of reduction, and, as quoted in the Globe and Mail of June 14, Dr. Rosenthal added a warning:
Venereal disease must be controlled in the future to the same extent as smallpox and diphtheria are today.
I again call your attention to the great need for research into the disease known as disseminated sclerosis. Some time ago I received three letters within the space of two weeks from comparatively young victims of this disease. It is a disease which not only incapacitates, but lasts for years, with attendant misery and suffering. I am glad to see that an organization has been set up to procure funds to stimulate research in the treatment of the disease, which is all too common. The Department of National Health and Welfare should give due consideration to the lending of all possible assistance to the prevention and treatment of disseminated sclerosis.
I now come to a subject which I have mentioned practically every year and at every session of parliament when the Department of National Health and Welfare estimates were being considered. I call your attention to the high cost of hospitalization, which is


Supply-Health and Welfare beyond the financial means of the average citizen. It is true that there has been increased tendency for people to seek hospital accommodation and treatment. It is very difficult at the present time to get help in the home; it is very difficult to get a trained nurse in order that the patient may receive the treatment that is necessary. There has been an increase in the building of hospitals and additions to hospitals, in order that more beds may be provided, but even with the grants given by the Department of National Health and Welfare, and also, in my own province of Ontario, the grants given by the provincial government for the building of hospitals and hospital beds, there is still a great shortage. Even with these grants it is difficult for cities, towns and municipalities to finance the building of hospitals and additions to existing hospitals.
Boards of hospitals have found it increasingly difficult to finance their institutions, even with these increased grants. It is necessary that we should have sufficient beds to meet the needs of our people. I am introducing a subject to which I hope the minister will give due consideration; the matter is very important. There should be sufficient hospital beds to meet the demand, in time of peace, and, which is more important, in time of war. Defence plans for the protection of our country must include adequate provision for our people in time of emergency. Modern warfare has shown the importance of making provision for civilians.
No review of the work of the Department of National Health and Welfare would be complete without mentioning the position of the so-called incurables. Many of these people are in the younger age groups. They are not able to earn their livelihood, owing to disease or accident suffered in earlier years. It is also possible that a percentage of this group could be helped in learning some form of gainful occupation. Many, because of their disability, find themselves unable to do any form of work. I am sure that the whole house will agree with me when I say that those people should receive assistance. It is only a short time since we had a group of them here. I am sure that every hon. member who saw them and interviewed them was impressed by the necessity of doing something for them, something that would give them a chance to lead- a normal life. As I looked at the group I felt that possibly some measures could be taken to train them in some work that they could carry on, even with their disability.
I draw attention, sir, to the remarkable work done in my own province of Ontario for the care of children or adults suffering from that dread disease poliomyelitis. All

cases in the province of Ontario are sent to selected centres for the period of isolation, which is only a matter of a week. Then they are sent to general hospitals for treatment after the infectious stage of the disease has passed, and it is possible to begin treatment of the affected muscles. Great work has been done in these centres toward the repair of and the bringing back to life of muscles which have been affected by the disease. This is all done at the expense of the provincial government. I wish to point out that it has paid rich dividends in preventing the crippling of many of these children. I have been impressed by the fact that children who have suffered from the disease, and who two or three years ago would have been left crippled for the rest of their lives, are now completely well, without any disability. Last summer one of my own patients, who was affected in both arms, back, and legs, received treatment at the Ottawa civic hospital, one of the selected hospitals for the treatment of this disease in Ontario. I am sure if it had not been for the modern methods of treatment which my patient received, she would have been a cripple for the rest of her life, on crutches or in a wheel chair. This patient is almost completely well, and in a few months time I am sure will recover from any form of disability.
So far as the disease itself is concerned, every effort should be made to foster research. The cause and the methods of prevention are not known, but much can be done by early measures of treatment to prevent crippling. I am well acquainted with the splendid results achieved in Ontario by a program of treatment of poliomyelitis victims, and I feel that the same type of program should be in effect in every province and every area in the Dominion of Canada. This program is so important that money from the dominion health grants should be allotted to the provinces for similar treatment. I hope that when I mention expenditures of that type no member on the government side will accuse me of advocating expenditures and at the same time advocating economy. There is no hon. member in this house who will quibble over the amount of money spent in the treatment or prevention or control of disease. The matter of economy rests in the administration of the department.
I now come to one of the most important matters under consideration this afternoon, namely, the expenditures of this department. It is the most expensive department of any in the government. The total amount required by the Department of National Health and Welfare is $455,253,570, with an increase of $44,557,114 as compared with the estimates of 1949-50. Some of these amounts are

authorized by statute. Large amounts are required for the payment of old age pensions and family allowances. It is not my purpose to criticize the amounts appropriated in any of these items; neither shall I criticize the amount spent on health services. Any government is justified in spending money on national health and welfare, and there is no department of the government that is as important as that which has to do with the care of the sick and the afflicted, or provision for the aged. Family allowances have done much for the younger aged group. The grants for the care of Indians and Eskimos of $11,694,839 have been necessary to preserve the health of the people who were the first inhabitants of this country. I could not under any circumstances criticize grants for such purposes as venereal disease control, mental health, blindness control and others, with the purpose of aiding the sick and afflicted. These grants are entirely necessary for the cure and prevention of disease, not only in the individual, but in the whole community. The individual and the whole community should be considered when we are dealing with sickness, particularly the treatment of a disease like tuberculosis.
But, sir, I have been amazed at the total amount of money required for travelling expenses in this department. I have made a summary of the travelling expenses in the various branches, and I am surprised to find that it reaches the grand total of $773,900, which is approaching the million mark. Supply-Health and Welfare to the last two wars a sum vastly in excess of what we spend on national health and welfare.
Above all, I hope the government will see to it that the grants for the treatment and prevention of some of the diseases that have been mentioned this afternoon will not only be maintained but increased, and that in the years to come we may look forward to great advances in the treatment of diseases that incapacitate and cause so much misery to so many people. It is satisfying to note that in some of our provinces many advances have been made in providing hospitalization. Having regard to their financial resources, I think some of the provinces have gone almost as far as they can go in providing, from their own resources, hospitalization and other health care.
As I said a few minutes ago, the time has come when the house should be considering a national health plan as a part of the social security program. I hope that the old age security committee will recommend a great advance in old age pensions, and I hope the government will accept their recommendation. When we have made this great advance then I think the problem to which we should give the highest priority in the next few years is a national health plan to make available to our people, as freely as our primary schools now are to our children, all the health services that the people of Canada require. I hope that such a plan can be developed in co-operation with the medical and nursing professions and all others interested in the problem, so that we shall not have a conflict of interests preventing or delaying the coming into effect of a great national health plan.
I am not going to say more this afternoon. I wish to support warmly the suggestions put forward by the hon. member for Lanark, and to say that we will support every measure proposed for the improvement of the general health and welfare of the people of Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my first words must be words of commendation to the minister and the Department of National Health and Welfare for the fine things they are doing in the fields of health and welfare for the purpose of improving living conditions and the happiness of the Canadian people. I have watched the work with keen interest, and I must say that in the past few years I have noted a real change in the attitude of the government of Canada to health and welfare matters. I enjoy listening to the hon. member for Lanark when he makes his contribution each year on the estimates of this department. A great deal of practical
[Mr. Coldwell.l
and down-to-earth information is always
to be found in the speeches he makes. Being a medical practitioner, his pronouncements naturally carry much more weight than they would coming from members who are laymen.
The members in this corner of the house have felt for many years that the governments of Canada were not doing enough in the fields of health and welfare. Every time the matter has come before the house we have demonstrated our concern in the only way that we could. We have made our proposals, and in the only government for which we have responsibility in this great dominion we have tried to demonstrate in a practical manner how we feel about health measures and public welfare. I think I am being modest when I say that in no province of the Dominion of Canada do the people enjoy more services in the field of health and welfare than they do in Alberta. We have been conscious of the need of the extension of those services. Even during the time, Mr. Chairman, when it was difficult to get money, when our total revenues in that province were less than $20 million, we did begin a gradual extension of health and welfare services; that has continued step by step right up to the present day. These health grants, hospitalization grants, construction grants, survey grants, have' all been of inestimable value to the province. We want to acknowledge those things, and to thank the minister for the leadership he gave in providing grants to the provinces. Without them many of the provinces could not have made the progress they have made; without them a good many more people would be suffering from the lack of hospital and other facilities within the field of health.
I do not want to take too much time, but there are a few things I should like to mention in connection with the estimates that are before us today. For a good many years, having had something to do with it in the administration of the province of Alberta, I have been keenly interested in the question of nutritional service. I have wondered just .how far the health department here integrates its investigation into nutritional problems with the research work going on in the Department of Agriculture, and the research council, as well as other agencies of government. I would appeal to the minister to do two things when he takes part in this debate: let us know just what is being done in that field to integrate the investigational services, and indicate to what extent the people ot Canada are being made aware of the findings of agencies of government.

I have discovered out of my own experience as a member of the provincial government that many of our people are actually starving to death in the midst of abundance. I do not mean that they are not getting their stomachs full of food that might perhaps look good, might perhaps be clean, might perhaps be sufficient in quantity; I simply mean that they are having to use so many devitalized foods. The flour the people of this country are getting is devitalized material; the very virtue has been taken out of it in the process of milling. It may be argued that the millers are giving the people what they demand, and that the people are actually demanding white, light flour; that may be so. If they are, it is done in ignorance. I am satisfied that a great many of the diseases suffered by the people of Canada today are deficiency diseases, and result from slow starvation arising from the use of foods that are devitalized, from which tne very elements the people need have been taken.
I should like to know how far the health department, along with other agencies of this government, has carried on research in nutrition, to discover exactly what has been happening and how to overcome the difficulty. In certain areas in this country the soil is worn out. Ordinarily, people in the cities are not aware that this is so. They are receiving in the markets of the cities vegetables and food materials that are grown on worn-out soil. These food materials are deficient in minerals. When human beings consume them it is only natural that they too should be deficient in tlfe minerals which they require, because the food itself does not contain what the people need for health. As a result we have an increase in the incidence of cancer, and a great many other diseases which doubtless will in time prove to be deficiency diseases. In nutritional research it seems to me that one of the important things to do is to determine from what areas food materials are coming that are deficient in mineral content, and if those are discovered the people of Canada ought to be warned of the results of consuming that food.
I have seen the publicity work. We ought to lay emphasis on that sort of information. I know some of the things that are being done. I have watched the bulletins that have come out of this department, and a great many of them are splendid. The pictorial nutritional charts especially have an appeal to many people. I do not begrudge one dollar that is spent on this sort of thing. We could lay emphasis on nutrition and get the people of Canada conscious of the necessity of producing and consuming vital food. Then I am satisfied you would not have to talk about
Supply-Health and Welfare hospitalization and the care of people who are falling by the way as a result of deficiency diseases.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
There are a good many things
I could say, but I would certainly say "amen" to that. My wife does make her own bread, and I do not care if the bakers know it.
I should like to add my voice to that of the leader of the C.C.F. party in his appeal to the minister and his colleagues to consider the plight of the incurables in this country. When the delegation representing the Canadian Association of Incurables visited Ottawa not long ago, they came to my office and spent some time in telling me their story. I must say, Mr. Chairman, that these people have a good case. I am satisfied that the minister knows that. They reported to me the sympathetic and fine reception the minister gave them. We all know that many of these incurables-no one knows how many hundreds of them there are-wish to be self-supporting. They constantly find themselves faced with this from employers: Now, we would like to give you work, but you would be an embarrassment or a danger around our institution. Their reflexes are not quick enough to handle mechanical operations, and sometimes it is difficult for them to move around. Amongst the delegation I found a number who expressed a desire to be independent. They told me their history- how they sought employment, and what their experience had been. My heart went out to them. I would say, sir, that their case is deserving of priority. I would think, in fact I will go so far as to say, that the needs of the incurables of this country are just as great as the needs of the old age pensioners or the blind; and while we are considering the extension of social services I say we should treat their requests on a par with those of the blind. It does seem, too, that it might be advisable not to put them under the Old Age Pensions Act, as we did the blind. I am of the opinion that we made a mistake in not drafting a special act for the blind, and I still believe that should be done at the earliest possible moment. I had something to do with the administration of old age and blind pensions in the province, and

Supply-Health and Welfare I concluded that we could have done a better job if there had been legislation specifically drafted covering the blind in this country. So I suggest that when we take up the question of the incurables-and we should do it immediately-we should draft an act particularly applying to them. One thing that surprised me about the whole situation was that thus far they have no way of determining exactly how many incurables there are in Canada, and for that reason it has been more difficult for them to lay emphasis upon their particular needs. I wonder if the minister, when he speaks, could tell us whether any move is being made by means of a survey across Canada to determine exactly how many incurables there are in need of financial assistance. If such information has not been gathered together thus far I think this should be done as soon as possible. Then we will be in a position to deal with the matter in terms of dollars and cents.
I should like to add my voice to the plea that has been made for further assistance, if it can possibly be made available, to the schools of social service. These schools are in need of assistance, and they are doing a good work. I believe they are deserving of much more help so that, as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said, they may be able to extend to prospective students bursaries or scholarships to encourage them to take up this work. It is of inestimable value to the Canadian people that trained social workers be available when they are needed; and today they are badly needed, if for nothing else than to help make our people conscious of the many things they could be doing for themselves. The true measure of the stability of a people and a nation lies in its ability to make use of the things that are at hand. Trained social workers are able to assist the>
people to learn exactly what is at hand and how to use it, and I think we should be laying some emphasis on that phase of our welfare work.
As the minister knows-and I do not intend to enter upon a long discussion of finance this afternoon-we in this group have tried to take a realistic position with respect to the expenditure of money. We have said that at the same time we are trying to extend health and social services we ought to be constantly mindful of the burden that has to be borne by the taxpayer, the ordinary consumer of this country. We have not retreated from that position by one inch. We say we will go along with the minister in everything he wants to do to improve the health conditions of our people and lessen the suffering of those who have been stricken. We urge him to go along just as 
quickly as he can, of course always being mindful of the taxpayers and the burden they have to bear. We have shown on numerous occasions, I think, that there is no lack of material wealth in this country. We have not begun to realize our productive capacity; and until we have realized our productive capacity we cannot say we have gone as far as possible in the extension of health and welfare services. It is out of our production that these things must come. If financial restrictions or a dearth of finances tend to interfere with the extension of these services, when at the same time we could produce more of the things that are needed, I say to the minister let us get out together and fight that sort of thing; let us remove the restrictions, get the materials into the hands of those who need them and the services to those for whom we are working now in connection with health and welfare.
We know what can be done because of the experience we have had in production. We know what this country is capable of doing. We urge the minister not to be too frightened by the size of the figures that may be presented to him by committees studying these matters. Let him rather take a look at the production end of it, the food, the clothing and shelter we could provide by all-out effort. Then let him govern himself accordingly, and we will back him to the limit.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the speeches that have been delivered in the house this afternoon have been characterized by a very constructive note, as well as by. a profound appreciation of the importance of the subject of national health and the kindred subject of national welfare. Since I agree with so much of what has been said, particularly by the hon. member for Lanark in his masterly speech, I believe I can shorten my remarks a good deal. The fact is that only last December, six months ago, the estimates of this department for last year were reviewed, and in addition during the present session the house has been afforded the opportunity of debating the subject of old age pensions on the motion to set up a special committee to go into that subject.
I should like to associate myself very heartily with what has been said on some aspects of the work of the department with which members of the committee on old age security have come directly in contact. I do not intend to discuss the subject referred to that committee, but I think tribute should be paid to the deputy minister, Dr. Davidson, to Miss Waters, Mr. Willard and other members of the staff who contributed so much to the material which was placed before that committee, comprehensive material which

reflected great credit upon those concerned in its preparation. I believe this tribute is well deserved.
Here we are dealing with a department whose proposed expenditures are the largest among all departments of government, with the exception of those coming under the Department of Finance. The hon. member for Lanark has drawn attention to the tremendous amounts proposed to be appropriated for travelling expenses in this department. I do not propose to discuss again that subject, with which he dealt so ably, but I do wish to draw attention to some other expenditures in this department which I think are worthy of note. In doing so I wish to make it quite clear that I have always been one of those who strongly supported the use of public moneys to meet national problems in relation to health and welfare, considering that when expenditures are directed to those purposes they are a valuable investment which will pay dividends in the national interest. But as members of this house it is our duty to be very sure that the taxpayer receives a dollar's value for every dollar spent, and that the moneys appropriated are voted consciously by parliament to assist in promoting the health and welfare of the nation.
Now, sir, I turn to a subject which has been discussed at previous sessions, but not always carried to the point of detail that it might well deserve. It is the subject of publicity. Anyone who examines this book of estimates must be impressed by the repeated appearances in the details in this book of that familiar title "Publicity", or under the more euphonious and impressive title which has been tagged onto it in recent years "Educational and Informational Publicity". That euphonious title deserves closer examination; the house should not be too greatly impressed by a resounding title. Let us go a little deeper, Mr. Chairman, and see exactly what is involved in these expenditures for this purpose.
First of all, as to the amount, I am sure it will surprise some to realize that in this department the items proposed to be spent on publicity during this present fiscal year total $524,970. How are they made up? Director of information services, $6,000; information officer, $4,080; and again under that same general heading we have $131,450 to be found under departmental administration. Then under the health branch, $66,000. We have an item under food and drugs. Chief of the advertising division-it may be that his salary should not be altogether charged to this subject, but I mention it in passing- $5,640.
Supply-Health and Welfare
Then we come to proprietary or patent *medicines, $7,000; opium and narcotic drugs, $2,000; child and maternal health, $44,500; public health engineering, $9,000; industrial health, $31,000; civil service health, $2,000; nutrition, $30,000; venereal disease control, $6,000; dental health, $13,500; mental health, $63,000; blindness control, $10,000; Indian medical service, $5,000; civil aviation medicine, $1,500. These are all under the health side of the department. Under the welfare side we have welfare branch, $2,500; family allowances, $56,500; and national physical fitness, $28,300. The total, as I have said, sir, is $524,970.
Let me make myself quite clear. I am not saying that there may not be good value in some of these expenditures. I am not making any general condemnation of expenditures on education, expenditures on certain forms of public information, which I think can properly be carried out through this department, but I think, sir, that in this very striking total there is money provided that ought to be very closely examined in this house. It is deplorable, sir, that this clumsy procedure we have available to us in this committee of supply does not enable hon. members to conduct that detailed examination which would be possible if we did take the intelligent course of setting up smaller committees to scrutinize estimates of this and other departments. But I do know, sir, that we have had occasion in the past to complain about some expenditures on these publicity items as being wasteful in their nature. We had an example the other day. It is true the minister's answer at page 3638 indicates that it is not a very large amount; but "Dietary Ditties" is not an isolated example, and as publicity it does not contribute very much to the public's awareness of health problems.

There is one other matter that, because of the profusion of items, cannot possibly be examined in the detail that the house should demand, having regard to the limited time here available. One will find scattered throughout the items of this department about twenty-five bearing the title, "sundries". These always sound like small items. That is not bad for sundries! The hon. member for Lanark suggests to me that it may be of assistance to those in the department who are travelling. I should like to offer only a brief word on the subject of health insurance. I had more to say on the subject on December 9 last when the estimates of this department were being considered. At that time I drew the attention of hon. members to the lamentable failure of the present administration to carry out the platform adopted by the Liberal party at its 1948 Ottawa convention, in relation to the inclusion of health insurance in its program of social security. This is the program that was adopted:
The program will include health insurance, covering medical, dental, surgical and hospital health services on a contributory basis.
There were no qualifications to that. There was no statement about waiting for another fifteen or twenty years; no suggestion about *deferring it for another generation. No, the statement was straightforward, direct and to the point. I have no doubt that in the election that took place one year ago this month that plank in the platform of the Liberal party was heeded by the people, with the thought that those who subscribed to it must have meant what they said.	*

What has been done? We
have asked the government repeatedly what it is going to do in relation to a national health program. We are still in the dark as to what plans, if any, the government has. The minister goes off on those long perorations about national health grants, and about waiting until the nation has digested them before he can even begin to tax his brains to carry out this promise in the Liberal platform, and meet a need which has been recognized by all parties in the house, namely the need for a national health program which will assure services of the kind here described to the people of this country.
We are waiting. We become impatient while we listen to nothing but excuses from the government for its inaction. The time has come for action. The minister is asked again to be concrete and definite, and to show some indication that action is intended. This year he has a golden opportunity in the dominion-provincial conference to meet this fall. This is an opportunity such as has not been made available to him for some time. Let him seize that opportunity. We have not had any intimation yet from the government that the subject of a health program is even to be included in the agenda of the conference. This is to be an exceedingly important gathering, and I do hope this opportunity will not be lost. There will be many things to be discussed before the conference; but here is something of major importance. I hope the minister will grasp this opportunity.
Let me point out to him that if he has cause for complaint about being misquoted concerning the intentions of the government in this field, much of the responsibility is attributable to the fact that the government has not been doing anything in the field. The minister complained in the house the other day about being misquoted. He pointed out that he had been quoted as having said in Vancouver on June 13 that he was against any national health insurance plan for Canada, and that health insurance is and must remain a provincial problem. In his statement to the house several days ago he remarked that he had not been correctly quoted in that press dispatch, and said he had subsequently given a statement to that same newspaper correcting their erroneous report.
Such misinterpretations and erroneous reports are bound to keep on turning up until the minister goes further than just to talk about the subject. The opportunity for misinterpretation will quickly disappear if he 55946-245

I should like to add my voice to those already heard today in the house about the problem of incurables, or those who are suffering from chronic diseases which incapacitate them from earning a living. All hon. members were impressed and touched by what we saw not only of the plight but of the courage of those who came to Ottawa a month ago representing the Canadian Association of Incurables. I take it that most hon. members have seen the brief which was submitted most competently on that occasion by Miss Eva Warden, and other spokesmen for the association of incurables. department and asks for information as to the number of persons in this unfortunate category, or what it would cost to provide some form of assistance to those who are in need of it and cannot help themselves, he will come away empty-handed, because there are no such statistics available in the Department of National Health and Welfare.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Peace
River mentioned a matter which to me seems important and vital. He mentioned that much of the food being consumed was deficient in minerals owing to soil deficiency, which perhaps was the reason for some of the diseases we are meeting today. I believe that is an


important point. I know that plants grown in deficient soil are stunted and sparse, and an animal fed on such plants has a hard time making progressive growth. It stands to reason that such an animal would not obtain sufficient minerals, and that would also be the case with the food product reaching the consumer.
Some time ago I mentioned in the house that farmers were very concerned about rebuilding their soil so that it would produce food containing the proper proportion of minerals. Today the farmers are not in the position to do that. They have been striving to produce cheap food, and in doing so have depleted their soil and allowed their buildings to get run down. They have produced cheap food, but it has been cheap not only in cost but in quality. Knowing that, and knowing that with the prices now being paid for agricultural products the farmers are not able to build up their soil, I believe we should seriously consider ways and means of placing the farmer in a position to replenish his soil so he will be able to produce food that will contain the minerals that are necessary if our people are to remain healthy.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
There is just one subject on
which I would like to say a few words on this general item of departmental administration, and that is the question of publicity and information. I should like to make it perfectly clear that I am not suggesting there are not certain departments in which information both as to the activities of the department and the progress being made in its work is perfectly legitimate and should be made available to the public. But while I believe that is true, and have no criticism of that type of information service, I have a deep-rooted objection to the use of information facilities within departments in order to put out not only government propaganda but partisan propaganda. The great difficulty is that departments and ministers find it so hard to resist the temptation to believe that what they are doing and the policies they are advocating and the government they are serving are the best. So it seems they cannot help publicizing not only their genuine departmental activities and services, but the points of view they espouse of a political as well as of an administrative nature.
That being so it appears that this tendency results, as we see from a comparison of today's spending with the past, in a constant increase in the amount being spent for publicity and information. This year the total being spent by all departments of government on publicity and information, as disclosed in the estimates, amounts to some $6 million. I gave the

exact figures in the course of an earlier speech, and they can be found in the record. When we are considering ways and means of reducing taxes I suggest that if we could find a way to reduce this expenditure without actually impairing the efficiency of the work and without depriving the public of genuine information to which it is entitled, that would be a worthwhile effort. Certainly one way it could be done is by cutting out the propaganda aspect of government information and publicity services.
I am going to urge that serious consideration be given a suggestion which has been made previously by myself and others; that is, that in order to control this expenditure for publicity and information throughout government departments a central bureau of information be set up, in the same way the printing bureau and the bureau for translations were set up, in order to do away with the overlapping and competition as between departments in connection with those services. We are now spending some $6 million a year on publicity, as far as we can ascertain from the estimates; but there are a number of hidden items, so the actual expenditure would be found to exceed $6 million if we had an accurate break-down. At any rate, we are spending $6 million now, and I am certain we could set up a bureau of information, give it half that amount of money and still produce all the genuine governmental information required to keep the people informed on those subjects as to which information is vital and essential in the national interest. I cannot conceive that it would not be possible to give all the service necessary along these lines at an expenditure of only half the amount now being spent under that heading, and certainly nothing has been said to show the contrary.
In this department we find that this year, according to those items which actually appear in the estimates, $524,970 is being asked for publicity and information. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that you can tell an awful lot of people an awful lot of things with more than half a million dollars, and that a good many of the things they are told are not genuine departmental information but political propaganda. 1 believe the setting up of a bureau of information, whose job it would be to sort out the requests of the departments for information services and see that no propaganda was put out but only genuine information, would be a powerful tool to cut down both the amount of propaganda going out and the expenditure under this heading.
Not only do I suggest that there is a certain amount of unwarranted and unnecessary
Supply-Health and Welfare information in the nature of propaganda going out from this and other departments;
I also suggest that some of the purely informational work is a waste of money, and the amount of it is Increasing constantly. I hold in my hand the annual report of the Department of National Health and Welfare, for 1949. Starting at page 132 of the report, seven pages are devoted to the detail of "Information services." When we find these large expenditures for publicity, with one department spending half a million
Supply-Health and Welfare dollars, then another department will almost inevitably say, "Our work is important, too. Look at the Department of National Health and Welfare, which is spending half a million dollars. Why do we not have more in our department to spend? Let us tell the people what we are doing". So in that way we find in this field a possibility of competition between departments. Indeed, the fact we are spending $6 million a year on publicity suggests it to be a reality. The setting up of a bureau of information or something along that line which would operate as a controlling factor before any information is put out would do much to eliminate the competitive aspect between departments and the improper spending of public money on political propaganda.

May I, at the outset, thank those hon. members who spoke particularly of the personnel in this department. No minister is better served, and I do not think any country is better served in the matter of health and welfare, through its public service, than is this country or than I am as Minister of National Health and Welfare.
May I first pay tribute to the staff-to all of them, including those who occupy senior posts and those who occupy the lowliest posts in the department-for what they are doing for this country. One does not like to mention names particularly, but because of the unusual distinction that comes with the designation of winner of the professional institute medal, let me say on behalf of the department how proud we were that the professional institute medal was this year given to one of the greatest men in the public health work of our country, Dr. Fred Jackson, director of health insurance studies.
A number of items have been discussed. The hon. member for Kamloops has referred to one in particular. It is all very well to say that we are spending too much on health information. No one is more concerned than I am about unnecessary expenditures in this particular. No one has taken greater care to see that in the opinion of my officers, of myself and of the provincial governments whatever expenditures we make in the field of health information are those which, after careful consideration, are thought to be expenditures that we should undertake.
No one has pointed out that the expenditures for health information this year have been reduced by over $73,000. One could make a strong case in criticizing that reduction. The speech of the hon. member for Peace River- I believe perhaps the finest speech this afternoon-urged us not to hesitate to use public funds to disseminate knowledge about health and welfare among our people. I took that as a challenge, and I will say this, that if any hon. member can show me one pamphlet or one film or one project carried on the information branch that should not be carried on, then I should like to have that suggestion made.
It is all very well to say we are spending too much money. But are we spending too much money when we have films telling the people of this country the ways and means of attacking mental illness? With respect to some of the titles to which my hon. friend referred, I do not criticize him for taking part in the debate in the lyrical and satirical way he did; that is perfectly natural -but the titles I must say are suggested by those who know how to reach the people.
Supply-Health and Welfare There is not one pamphlet, not one film undertaken by the Department of National Health and Welfare that is not approved by all the provinces sitting in at the annual conference of the health educational divisions across this country.
Then, with regard to the other projects, apart from certain publications we have taken over from the national welfare council, it will be found that all the publications, all the films and other projects have been recommended by the dominion council of health. Twice each year all the provincial governments meet with us here in Ottawa, incidentally at our expense, to discuss ways and means of co-ordination in the field of health activities. They meet with us to discuss ways and means of avoiding duplication and overlapping.
Let me say that there is no sphere of government where co-operation between the provinces and the dominion is as effective and as continuous as in the fields represented by the dominion council of health. In addition to that, I have a committee in our department that goes over matters carefully, and reviews the technical aspects as well as the effectiveness of distribution.
I know what my hon. friend does not like. The fact is that in this Department of National Health and Welfare we are doing something for the people of Canada. The fact that we have taken ways and means to let the people know what we have done proves a little irritating to some hon. members -just as it would to me, if I were sitting over there.
The hon. member has referred to travelling expenses. The travelling expenses in this department are large, but they are not by any means the largest of any government department. I believe we would stand about sixth in the extent of our expenditures in this connection. But is there a department in which the obligation to travel is greater? I certainly do not feel, for one, that I am a good Minister of National Health and Welfare unless I get around this country and see for myself what should be done. That I propose to continue to do. I do not think, further, that my officials are doing their jobs unless they, too, carry on a program of visiting the centres, dealing with the provinces, dealing with the hospitals, dealing with our food and drug administration, dealing with our narcotics administration and the like.
Let us examine this travelling expenses vote to which reference has been made. Of the increase over last year, some $60,000 is due to the increased expenditures incurred in taking Indians from more remote areas of

Supply-Health and Welfare our country to hospitals for hospitalization and medical attention. Of the total, $208,000 -I am using round figures-is spent in the transportation of sick Indians to hospitals. Other expenditures are necessary for the travelling of the dominion council of health and the Canadian council of nutrition, bodies which are representative of the provinces; and also for the transportation of sick mariners to hospitals, a statutory obligation. Then there is the cost of delegates to the second assembly world health organization, which it was suggested was a wrong thing to approve.
Then there are the courses taken in connection with civil aviation, medicine and the travelling expenses of our food and drug inspectors. Last year only $34,000 was spent and there was criticism by the drug council that we were not keeping up with the situation. One reason was that we had not enough inspectors. However, the number is now up to around forty. There are also the travelling expenses of the narcotic inspectors and the quarantine medical officers who are engaged in the inspection of aircraft and vessels.
Then there are medical officers who are engaged in the inspection of prospective immigrants. There are also the field officers of the public health engineering branch. We are trying to do something to improve the quality of the drinking water consumed in this country and the water available in our trains, aeroplanes, stations and public buildings is inspected by these officers in co-operation with the provincial officers. I suggest that we should carry on that kind of work.
Then there are the officers of the family allowances division who make inspections to see that the money is not being misspent. We are spending $309 million this year and travelling expenses of around $39,000 is not an overestimate or overexpenditure. There are the travelling expenses of the old age pension auditors and the child and maternal health division officers, which is I submit a legitimate expense. We would not be doing our job in this department, as I have been told on previous occasions by hon. members opposite that we were not, if our officers were not travelling around in the performance of their duties.
Then there is the Indian health service which requires the transportation of the field staff of doctors and patients. Within five years our expenditures on Indian health have gone up six times. We have 21 hospitals all over the country, with nursing stations. Then there are the doctors on part time who are assisting us in this work. All this requires travelling, and I submit necessary travelling.


The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar in his excellent statement, which was supported by the hon. member for Glengarry, referred to the importance of nutrition. Incidentally the head of our nutrition branch is an Albertan which should give confidence to the hon. member for Peace River who has made some observations. We are making nutrition surveys continuously and at times the amount of travelling involved is very heavy. But it is necessary to carry on this important work.
Industrial health surveys are now being made in the province of Quebec and in the maritime provinces in connection with silicosis and the like. This entails travelling by the officers if the job is to be done. We are now making a dental health survey which involves travelling expenditures. Also a morbidity survey is being undertaken.
One can talk about the work of the regional directors of family allowances and the work of our senior departmental officers in connection with the health branch. There are officers who are continually in touch with the provinces, not only by letter but more particularly by telephone and personal contact. Dr. Jackson and his staff are repeatedly in contact with the provincial governments in connection with the national health program. It takes time and patience on the part of all concerned to set up such a program and there is need to have men all over the country, in some instances trying to persuade provincial officers to co-operate or trying to persuade provincial authorities as to the desirability of sending in projects. There is a need of personnel in many branches of health work and our officers try to supply that at all times.
I think the explanation that the increase in travelling expenditures is due mainly to the transportation of Indians from remote areas to the hospital centres is one that will commend itself to every hon. member of the committee. No reference was made to the decrease that has occurred in travelling expenditures by many divisions. There is a decrease in travelling estimates in national health branch administration, in the immigration medical service, in the child and maternal health division, in the public health engineering division, in the civil service health division, in the nutrition division, in the mental health division, in welfare branch administration and in departmental administration.

speechtext: Is that as compared with last year's expenditures or estimates?
