speechtext:
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar raised a matter of great interest -I cannot discuss all the matters that were

raised-which I think deserves further attention. He referred to disseminated sclerosis and the need to do something about that disease. I told him last year that we were giving consideration in our research grants to a project to deal with that very thing. There are now two research projects under way in the field, one at Queen's university and one by the Saskatchewan health department. The cost of both projects is being borne entirely by the federal government.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
What amount is being
appropriated?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I have not the total amount, but the projects were sent in by the provinces.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
What is the federal
contribution?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
The total cost is being borne by us. I have not the figure right here but I shall get it. Then the hon. member referred to the Montreal Neurological Institute. I was able to tell this house two years ago of an annual grant that we were going to make toward the work of Dr. Penfield, a work which is of national and international significance. I am happy to say that this year we have supplemented that by an equipment grant of $173,000. I am happy to say that we are giving consideration to making a hospital construction grant to that particular institution. Anything that we can do to help that institution will not go undone.
Reference was made to sundries and the hon. member for Eglinton suggested that we were spending some $200,000 for sundries. Let us see what that represents. Of that expenditure, $130,000 or approximately 60 per cent is to cover laundry services for the Indian medical services where departmental laundries do not exist or would be impracticable. For instance, at Edmonton and Nanaimo laundry costs run about $30,000 a year. You cannot build hospital facilities and nursing centres unless these expenditures are made.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: In a case like that why should it not be shown that the expenditure is for laundry services?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
There is no primary item for that. Perhaps consideration will be given to giving that information in that way. I merely mention that to indicate the real story of the sundries item. Reference was made to the grant to schools of social work. This year we are making a grant of $52,500. Hon. members have written to me suggesting that this is not a large enough amount to cover the important work that the schools of social work are doing. I recognize the importance of the work because the personnel of
Supply-Health and Welfare my department to be efficient inevitably must be made up of people who have not only the training gained through experience but also the knowledge that comes from formal education. It was for that reason that this grant, which was started during the war, has been continued. Whether or not it will be increased will be a matter that will have to rest with the government as a whole, and our policy in that regard will have to be announced in due course.
As to the question of incurables, I saw the delegation to which the hon. member referred when it was here. I agree with the hon. member for Peace River that one could not help noticing their disabilities and recognizing the great and almost prior social claim that they have upon those of us in the government and outside because of the particular handicaps under which they are suffering. For personal reasons I feel very keenly about this matter, as hon. members well know. I take second place to no man in my desire to set in motion-and I cannot speak any more succinctly or finally on this subject-something that I trust and hope will, in the course of not too long a time, afford some relief to these people.
We have made a start. In the first place I do not recognize that the problem is solely our responsibility. I will not argue now as to whose responsibility it is. I think it is clear that in this country we do not want to overcentralize in the government at Ottawa, either in terms of policy or in terms of administration, matters having to do with either health or social welfare. Certainly that is my view. The provinces, the municipalities and voluntary bodies have a responsibility as to the handicapped, or incurables, as they are sometimes called.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Within their financial ability.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Yes, and within ours too. I
do not feel I am doing my duty if I do not constantly emphasize that all these meritorious things in the field of health and social welfare have to be paid for, and there is only one way by which most of us recognize they can be paid for, out of the hard work of the people. Recognizing the importance of this matter, we have instituted a sickness survey that will begin shortly. It will be carried out by the provinces with the total expense to be borne by us. Its purpose is to ascertain (a) the number of incurables and (b) the number who are non-income earning, so that we can make an assessment of the problem and be able to know exactly what the problem is. Having made that assessment, we will be in a more intelligent

Supply-Health and Welfare position to formulate a policy alone or in collaboration with the other governments of the country.
In addition, as the house knows, at the instance of the Minister of Labour, the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the Minister of National Health and Welfare a conference on rehabilitation was called to meet on May 25 last. All provincial governments, certain voluntary bodies and certain organizations representing the incurables and the handicapped had agreed to come. Unfortunately the Manitoba flood caused the governments of Saskatchewan and Manitoba to request a postponement of the conference. Under the circumstances they could not allow their officials to attend such a conference at that time, important as it was. It was not because those provinces were not interested but because a prior obligation had suddenly seized them. I am hoping that the conference can take place at the earliest possible moment for the purpose of exploring the position that must be taken as to this most important problem, one which has, as I say, not only a great appeal but a great claim on our sympathy.
Reference was made to the question of health insurance, and my views on this subject are well known. There is the question of the burdensome cost of hospital care, drugs, and what I might call ancillaries of that character, together with medical expenses, and I have put them deservedly last, I think. Not recognizing the situation in specific instances, but recognizing the burden of these things, I have put medical expenses last, not in terms of importance but in terms of what it means by way of economic burden on the majority of the people of Canada. I believe, as I have always believed -and I am now speaking personally-that the problem of sharing the cost of health care can be met effectively by a system of health insurance. One has to recognize that in the pursuit of that objective there are certain important circumstances to consider.
I believe one of these is that nothing should ever be done to interfere with the doctor-patient relationship that has become a tradition in this country. I think anything that would interfere with the autonomy-and I mean that in the professional sense-of the doctor would be serious not only for the doctor but more particularly for the cause of good health in this country.
I feel I should say that because it is so often suggested that the intention is to make doctors simply servants or salaried officers of the state. I believe it is important to


maintain the doctor-patient relationship. It is also important to recognize, if we are going to develop a satisfactory plan, that under the constitution the primary responsibility for health rests with the provincial governments. Some may argue that the situation should be otherwise, but that is the constitutional fact. I respect it, and I think in terms of administration it is a good thing, as well as from the point of view of developing a sound policy. I believe all these things must be carefully considered. As we go forward step by step with our social security program, we will want to make sure that each step is taken responsibly and carefully in the light of all the circumstances in order to avoid retrenchment or abandonment of programs later on which might prove disastrous, as so many hon. members know.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre referred to the proposals made by the government in 1945 which involved the recognition of the collaborative possibilities of action between the provinces and the federal government. I made a statement in this house not so long ago which I repeat, that a national health plan, in the language of the former prime minister and repeated by his successor, is looked upon as a fundamental prerequisite to the establishment of a national system of health insurance. It is all very well to say that we can wait too long for our services to be built up. One hon. gentleman said that our services were being built up now, and in the next breath he complained that we were not building them up fast enough. The fact is that we have in the past two years, in collaboration with the provinces, built over 20,000 hospital beds. Our objective was 40,000 hospital beds in five years. In less than two and a half years we have exceeded half of our total objective. We are training personnel in all branches of health activity; in the field of mental health; in the field of tuberculosis control; in the field of crippling conditions in children. We have increased the number of health units. When I say "we have increased," the provinces have recommended to us projects which call for the increase of public health units, and we have paid the cost of those additional health units that are being built all over the country at the suggestion of the provinces and administered by them.
All of these public health units are a very important phase in the development of a program by which we will attempt, I hope in a responsible way, to meet what undoubtedly is a great economic burden on the masses of the people of this country. When you think

that at the moment we are training undei that plan over 1,500 individuals, giving them post-graduate training; training in particular phases of research, and in particular phases of public health administration, you will realize the tremendous transition that is taking place. I hope, and I believe, it is taking place along responsible lines towards the improvement of the health services, as a condition precedent to the next step. When one thinks that we have made it possible for the provincial governments alone to Increase their personnel by over 2,000 individuals, one will appreciate the great preparatory steps that are being taken in connection with this matter. One could go on reciting the achievements that are the result of the joint effort of provincial and federal governments in the execution of a national health program. I have only touched a few of the highlights but they are significant in more ways than one, not only on the research side but what is being done, for instance, in the province of Saskatchewan. In that province there is a project, signed only the other day, concerning the second phase of a dental health program in the schools. One could mention the assistance that we are giving to arthritic sufferers through the arthritic and rheumatism society in British Columbia. One could single out of all these things many examples of what is being done. In other words what I am seeking to establish, and to impress upon the house, is that we are building a whole series of medical services in this country that will place us in a very strong position once we have to deal with the broader problem in collaboration with the provinces, upon whom, under our constitution, rests the primary responsibility.
I repeat now what I said to the house. "This program would have the added advantage of being the fundamental prerequisite of a nation-wide system of health insurance. Indeed, this program represents the first stages. The new services being developed and the new hospitals being built with these federal grants are hastening the moment when in every province it will be possible to consider further action towards hospital and medical care insurance-for which, of course, the federal government stands ready to provide assistance, under satisfactory agreements for dominion-provincial co-operation." Then, I associated that with a statement made by the Prime Minister in a radio address in which he said:
It is up to the people and the government in each province to take the initiative in working out health insurance plans in line with their local conditions and their traditions.
Supply-Health and Welfare
Anyone who has had anything to do with provincial administration or with federal administration would recognize that that statement was nothing but an important one, particularly in the light of the present character of dominion-provincial relations in this country.
Mr. Chairman, there were many other matters to which reference was made by the various members. I may be overlooking quite a number of them. All I hoped to do in this initial statement was to generally deal with some of the problems that have been mentioned. The Department of National Health and Welfare has assumed increasing importance. Our total expenditure proposed for this year amounts to $455 million. The main part of that total is made up of uncontrollable items. Over ninety per cent of the expenditures of this department are for family allowances, old age pensions and certain statutory obligations such as food and drugs and narcotics control. This covers the work being done by the department in the various fields that are created either by statute or by provincial agreements, and leaves less than ten per cent of the departmental activities that one may consider in the controllable class.
When one examines that controllable class, one finds that in fact most of the expenditures are uncontrollable. There is first of all the money that is being spent on Indian health; there is the money that is being spent on a national health program. That leaves only four and one-half million dollars in the health branch that can again be regarded under the heading of "controllable." Out of that four and one-half million dollars the Department of National Health and Welfare is left with only $1,200,000 to engage in matters of health on a co-ordinating basis with the provinces. Instead of saying that we are spending too much in the field of health, I am forced-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: No one has said that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
No, I said that instead of saying that, I am forced to affirm that I do not believe this represents by any means an undue expenditure in trying to bring about co-ordination in all the fields of health activities with the provinces. It is true that the national health program this year, which makes $34 million available to the provinces, does open up a channel of opportunity which I know commends itself to the house, just as I believe it commends itself to most people in this country.
At six o'clock the Speaker resumed the chair and the house took recess.

subtopic: EXCHEQUER COURT TO HAVE JURISDICTION IN ACTIONS ORIGINATING IN QUEBEC AND NEWFOUNDLAND

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, June 13, consideration of the motion of Mr. Knowles for the second reading of Bill No. 13, to provide for the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court of Canada in matters of divorce.

maintopic: DIVORCE JURISDICTION
subtopic: EXCHEQUER COURT TO HAVE JURISDICTION IN ACTIONS ORIGINATING IN QUEBEC AND NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, practically every member of this house you speak to privately is of the opinion that this matter of divorce should be taken out of the House of Commons and Senate. That is their private opinion. Some hon. members and a section of the press look upon this matter from a straight sectarian standpoint, and are of the opinion that this bill contains the principle of divorce as such. As far as I am concerned my religious persuasion places me in the position that I am unalterably opposed to divorce as such, but I do not see this bill in that category.
From time to time those in the other place have registered their disapproval of the method employed in the granting of divorce in the province of Quebec. From what you hear emanating in the other place they would like to be relieved of this responsibility. As I said before, this is not a question of deciding on the principle of divorce. That has

been decided already. Whether we like it or not we have divorce, and as far as I am concerned all this bill seeks to do is devise some other means more in keeping with our times than the way it has been done in the past. We have divorce now; so the argument that by passing this bill and shifting responsibility from the Senate and House of Commons to the exchequer court, in effect we would be deciding the principle of divorce and registering approval of it, in my opinion is quite wrong.
For several sessions I served on the committee on miscellaneous private bills, to which these bills are referred. During my years of service on that committee I opposed all these bills in cases where children were involved. Under the method now followed in the province of Quebec, if you have a legal separation there are institutions that will maintain the children if the parents are not prepared to do so. As soon as you go to the Senate, however, and obtain a divorce you are legally divorcing the children in that province from the maintenance now provided under the separation arrangements.
I do not think it is true to say that passing this responsibility over to the exchequer court would increase the number of divorces in Quebec. We handle some 300 divorces a year coming from that province, and if you will take the province of Ontario, which is most nearly comparable to Quebec, you will find that year by year the divorce ratio in Quebec is equal to that of Ontario.

maintopic: DIVORCE JURISDICTION
subtopic: EXCHEQUER COURT TO HAVE JURISDICTION IN ACTIONS ORIGINATING IN QUEBEC AND NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: DIVORCE JURISDICTION
subtopic: EXCHEQUER COURT TO HAVE JURISDICTION IN ACTIONS ORIGINATING IN QUEBEC AND NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Oh, yes; so if they went to a court it would not affect the matter one way or the other. I want to have it understood- I have already voted for the bill-that I am still in favour of it. If the matter is handled by the exchequer court-the court is there now, and I do not think it is too busy-at least those seeking divorce would not receive the publicity that they do at the present time. While we stand up in the house and speak and vote against crime comics and obscene literature, the three hundred divorce bills that go through year after year and the published evidence that is circulated in the House of Commons and to some extent through the country are, in my opinion, much worse than any of the literature that you could pick up on the newsstands. By shifting from one government institution, or two government institutions, the problem of handling divorce to another government institution we are certainly not deciding on the principle of divorce, because we have divorce now. I think this bill proposes a better device and a better method of handling divorce, until such time as it is decided in some other way than it is handled at the present time.
Divorce Jurisdiction

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DIVORCE JURISDICTION
subtopic: EXCHEQUER COURT TO HAVE JURISDICTION IN ACTIONS ORIGINATING IN QUEBEC AND NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
I do not intend to take very long, and I am not rising to talk this bill out, but to bring before the house certain facts that have not been alluded to in this debate though they were brought before the house on a former occasion when a similar bill was introduced.
There is no doubt that under the British North America Act parliament has jurisdiction with respect to divorce. That is one of the express provisions of the act. There is also no doubt that before confederation there were in force in the province of Quebec laws which by virtue of the British North America Act continue in force until they are amended or repealed by the jurisdiction having authority to deal with them. That is to be found in the explicit terms of section 129 of the British North America Act.
Among the laws which were in force in the province of Quebec, and which have not been dealt with by the legislature of Quebec or by this parliament up to the present time, and which continue to be in force, is section 185 of the Quebec civil code. That is in force in the province of Quebec, and it is not in force anywhere else, and any legislation to deal with it is legislation for the province of Quebec and for the province of Quebec alone.
That section of the code is very clear, and I think the shortest way to bring its content before hon. members is to read it. It is as follows:
Marriage can only be dissolved by the natural death of one of the parties: while both live, it is indissoluble.
Such is the Quebec law at the present time, and until that law is amended or repealed, the matter is not one of who will have jurisdiction to hear a divorce case; the matter to be dealt with consists of a fundamental declaration of the law and that is why the hon. member who introduced this bill took the precaution to declare that the exchequer court would have jurisdiction and would have the right to dissolve a marriage. That however would be legislating for the province of Quebec. It would be within the power of this parliament, but still it would be legislating on a matter which is extremely distasteful to the large majority of the people of that province. I can understand that it may not be agreeable for the houses of parliament to have to deal with these individual cases which are brought up from year to year. But parliament does deal with them, and the manner in which it deals with them does give satisfaction to those who believe that there should be a legal procedure for obtaining dissolution of a marriage. That is something which has been going on ever since confederation, and which has created no controversial issue

Divorce Jurisdiction
between the majority in my province and the majority in other provinces who may or may not believe that divorce is a good thing, or that divorce is an inevitable evil.
But this proposal to legislate contrarily to the terms of section 185 of the Quebec civil code will be strongly resented on religious grounds by the very large majority of the people of the province of Quebec.
We have made considerable progress in recent years toward national unity, and the matter now being debated is something which would be felt by a large number as being an imposition by a majority of a law that the people of the province of Quebec do not want. Why do it? Simply because it would relieve us here of the painful duty of having to consider these individual divorce bills, why create that controversy and disturb a situation with which I think most Canadians are satisfied, why disturb the good relations and tolerant attitude of each sector of the population toward the other sectors of the population?
I submit that we should continue, as our predecessors have done, to deal with the individual cases rather than have parliament exercise its jurisdiction, and pass an act which would bring an exception to the application of this general law and in one fell swoop take this general law out of the civil code of Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, since the Prime Minister has said something on this bill I should like to say a word regarding the other place handling divorce bills. In the Senate the members who are on the divorce committee have to sit whether the Senate is sitting or not. In justice to these men who faithfully stay on the job I personally feel that some consideration should be given to them for the work they have done and1 are doing.
Just a short time ago I heard that one man has failed in health owing to the fact that he had been on the divorce committee so long. I think something should be done for them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
maintopic: DIVORCE JURISDICTION
subtopic: EXCHEQUER COURT TO HAVE JURISDICTION IN ACTIONS ORIGINATING IN QUEBEC AND NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have always been opposed to the present method of handling divorce cases; I am still opposed to it. I think we ought to get away from the granting
(Mr. St. Laurent.)
of divorces by a special law in each case. I cannot see that there is any good reason why a woman who has had a certain amount of trouble with her husband should come to parliament and ask to have a law passed for her special benefit; or that a man who has had trouble with his wife-the trouble in each case getting to the point of one of them committing adultery-should expect parliament to pass a law for his benefit. I do not think it should be expected by either of them. Parliament should not pass for them individually a law saying they are no longer married, and that they may marry again. More especially is this so perhaps when our law cannot say anything about children or about property.
While I am opposed to the method we are following, I certainly cannot follow the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) in the proposal he has put before the house. I agree with what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has said, that we should not do anything that would tend in a way to destroy or to injure the unity of this country.
What the bill proposes is to force divorce as a general law upon the province of Quebec, something which is anathema to the people of that province. I cannot see any wisdom, I cannot see any fairness or any fair play in saying to the people of Quebec, "You do not like divorce? Well, you will have it. We are giving it to you. We are now passing a law against what we know to be your wishes, whereby you will have divorce. You will all have it, and you will get it in a court". But the bill does not say merely that the exchequer court may grant some divorces; that it may pick and choose, as we do in the House of Commons and in the Senate. Here we let an individual come forward and we pass a law for her or, if it is a man, we pass a special law for him. What this bill says is that all who would may come to the exchequer court, and that it will grant divorce. "We will force it-that is what we will do; we will force it upon the people of Quebec". That is where I part company with the sponsor of this legislation. I do not believe in the method we are following. I think that ought to stop. I do not see any reason whatever for passing a special law for John Doe in the province of Quebec or in the province of Newfoundland. It he did not check about divorce laws before he went to live in Quebec, that is his lookout. If he wishes to live in a place where there is divorce, then let him move to that place and establish domicile. But I do not see that he ought to have any right to come here and have a special law passed for him.

But if anybody else agrees with that, then the only thing to do is to stop passing these laws, and not to say that in order to get away from passing these laws we are going to arrange it so that anyone who wishes and if the grounds exist may go to the courts and get a divorce-to the exchequer court if he lives in the province of Quebec. Surely that is not the way to cure my objection to the legislation.
The way to cure the objection I have is simply to stop. And I would point out to the hon. member for Cape Breton South that if he and two or three of his friends wished to do so, they could stop every one of these divorce bills going through the House of Commons. There is no doubt about that. After the experience the house had with the pipe line bills, everyone must agree that the C.C.F. party, for example, if it wished to stop every one of these divorce bills-unless, of course, the house were to change its rules- could do so. I am in that position myself, although I am opposed to it and do not see fit to follow that course because so many others are in disagreement with me. But if there are others who feel as strongly about it as the hon. member for Cape Breton South appears to feel, he and they have it pretty well in their own hands to stop these divorces.
While I do not expect there will ever be a majority who will hold my point of view, that we should simply stop, I do hope there will always be a very large majority who will say that they will not force upon Quebec this legislation which is, as I have said, anathema to the people of that province.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) were to speak now he would close the debate, I should like to say a word at this time.
I am opposed to the bill for the reasons given by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), but certainly not for the illogical reasons just given by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank). Every argument he advanced against the exchequer court's having jurisdiction could be applied with equal force in other ways. He said, in effect, in the words of the old hymn, "Whosoever will may come." That is the situation now, and giving jurisdiction to the exchequer court does not change that one iota. Anyone can come here just as easily as and perhaps more easily than he can go to the exchequer court.
I am opposed to the change for this reason: I believe the people of the province of
Divorce Jurisdiction
Quebec are overwhelmingly against divorce as such, but they have expressed themselves by the majority of their members here as being content, to some extent in any event, with the procedure we now have. I am still one of those peacemakers who are really hopeful of unity in this country of which all of us are very proud. I say to the people who are advocating this change: let us get over this idea that there must be a law to cover everything on which we disagree. Laws are general things; they are big things. There are special acts; but why anyone now, to use the language of the street, would want to throw a monkey wrench into the machinery is beyond my understanding.
I have my own ideas with respect to these matters. I am one of those people who believe in divorce. I am not going to give my reasons, because we have all heard them so often. But, for the sake of Canadian unity, let us not deliberately stir up a nest of hornets, which we could easily do by passing this legislation and, in effect, say to the people of those two provinces, "We are doing this, knowing that the majority of your people are opposed to it." I would go that far if it were a matter of great principle of general application. That would not disturb me at all, if the people of one province took a course which, we will say, might be detrimental to the interests of the other provinces. But for the sake of that Canadian unity to which we all aspire let us not bring in something which may do it harm and which will not do one bit of good for those individuals who are seeking divorce. Therefore I am opposed to the bill as presented.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I well recall a few years ago after there had been quite a few speeches by members of the house objecting to parliament having to deal with divorce, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), who was then minister of justice, made the suggestion that those who were complaining about the present practice should suggest an alternative. As a matter of fact, he did outline a possible modification himself although he made it quite clear that he was not necessarily advocating it. It was because of the challenge given by the Prime Minister when he was minister of justice that I had this bill drafted. It was not drafted this year or last year, it was drafted several years ago. I kept it in my files for some years before placing it on the order paper. I placed it on the order paper with the sincere desire, for which some hon. members have given me credit, of dealing with this matter which is obnoxious to all of us in this parliament, no matter where we sit.
As the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has said, hon. members on all sides of the house, privately as well as publicly, have complained because we have this practice here. I think it is true to say that hon. members generally wish that there was some other way to deal with this matter. I think I am justified in paraphrasing what the Prime Minister said when he was minister of justice by saying to those who are opposed to this bill, "All right, suggest some other alternative to the present practice. You do not like my bill, you do not like what we are doing; surely then there must be some other solution to the problem you can suggest."
When I introduced the bill I indicated that it was not the kind of bill that we in this corner usually introduce, that it was not a bill containing some basic and fundamental principle of social philosophy to which we were firmly attached and from which we would not budge. I indicated that it was merely an attempt to solve a problem of parliament and I said also that I would be quite happy if someone were to move an amendment that the bill be not now read a second time, but that the subject matter thereof be referred to a special committee of the house. I knew that if that course were followed it would mean the killing of my bill so far as this session was concerned but it would make possible a discussion in a committee of the subject matter, indeed of the whole problem of what should be done to relieve parliament of this obnoxious practice.
It may be that I did not get my suggestion about an amendment across to hon. members; at any rate it was not taken up. It is in my

own mind at the moment that at the next session it might be worh while to introduce the bill again and make sure that such an amendment is moved. That again would have the effect of killing the bill for that session but it would make possible a discussion of the whole problem in a special committee of the house.
I am sure that my speaking in this fashion makes it crystal clear, although it did not need to be made clear, that my purpose is not to stir up any disunity, that my purpose is not to jam something down the throat of anyone in this country who does not want what he thinks is involved in this bill; my purpose is simply to solve a problem that faces parliament, the solution of which we have the right to seek.
Since some arguments have been put forward I feel I should answer them. I was interested in hearing the Prime Minister give us the terms of section 185 of the Quebec civil code. He suggested that if this bill were to pass it would be an attempt by parliament to override the provisions of that section. Every time we pass a divorce bill we do just that, and no effective opposition is put forth. I know hon. members make a fine distinction between each and every divorce bill as it comes along as being a special case as contrasted to a general act, but I submit that what happens in this parliament is that two hundred or three hundred times a year we override section 185 of the Quebec civil code when we dissolve a marriage, despite the fact that that section says that a marriage shall not be dissolved so far as Quebec persons are concerned except by the death of one of the parties.
The same argument has been put forward by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin), by the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier) and by other hon. members who have spoken in this debate. They admit that this bill does not provide any facility for divorce not now available to the people of Quebec or Newfoundland, but they have pointed out publicly and they have pointed out privately to me-and I appreciate the manner in which these members have discussed this matter with me-that in their view there is a difference between providing for divorces in the exchequer court and having divorces granted by parliament. They point out that every divorce act is a special case, a sort of emergency. When we grant three hundred divorces a year, surely it is not a special case every time. Indeed, we are becoming a mill. We are more of a divorce court than the divorce court itself.

I suggest that to transfer the handling of these matters from the Senate and the House of Commons, where they are out of place and where neither the Senators nor we like them, to a court where they can be dealt with more properly is a sensible and intelligent course to follow. It would not make divorce easier; it would not change the basis for divorce. As a matter of fact, it might make the obtaining of a divorce a little more difficult. Some of the applicants to the exchequer court might not find it as easy to get a divorce there as they would by going through the routine before the Senate committee. Any who have taken the trouble to read some of the salacious documents you get from there know how routine the proposition is.
I felt that I should say something to make it clear that this bill in no way imposes upon the sensibilities or the feelings of the people of Quebec. The fact is that three hundred times a year we override the Quebec civil code, and I think the procedure outlined in the bill would be much more sensible.
In listening to the various arguments that have been put forward, I felt there was one advanced by the hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Kent) on May 26 which should be considered. He pointed out something of which I was aware and which I realize my bill does not fully take care of. He pointed out that the exchequer court can sit anywhere in Canada and as a matter of fact does sit in various parts of the country. He pointed out that it was a circuit court, and that there was nothing in the bill to prevent the exchequer court from actually sitting within the boundaries of the province of Quebec for the purpose of dealing with divorce cases. I recognize that could be offensive. I would say that if my proposal were carried out there should either be an understanding or, better still, it should be written into the bill that the exchequer court would sit only in Ottawa to deal with divorce cases from the two provinces concerned.
I feel that the other arguments advanced are matters of opinion. I think that some consideration should be given to the sensibilities of members of parliament. I do not think we should be asked to go on and on through the years pursuing a practice which is obnoxious to us. After all, if I may use the language that appears in the title of every divorce bill, the bill now before the house really is an act for the relief of parliament.
I do not intend to proceed further. I want to say quite clearly, in case there should be any thought that the bill has the effect of creating disunity, that it is not my purpose to force a recorded vote on the measure when I conclude what I have to say. If you hear
Divorce Jurisdiction
more yeas than nays, Mr. Speaker, I shall be quite happy. If you hear too many nays and declare the motion lost that will be the end of the bill so far as this session is concerned, but I hope we will not go on forever following a practice which all of us find offensive, and which all of us feel is out of keeping with the purposes of parliament.
I say again that the purpose of the bill was certainly quite clear, that it was not to impose upon any group of people in Canada anything that is not now available to them. It is already there-shall I say, it is already here. In this building there is what amounts to a permanent divorce court for the people of the provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland. As the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) said to the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank), everyone in those two provinces who wants to can come to this supreme court of divorce, this parliament building, and get a divorce. I think some day the practice should be changed. If perchance my accepting the challenge of the Prime Minister some years ago to those of us who did not like the practice to devise some means of getting around it leads to a challenge to others to find some better means than I have proposed, I shall be quite happy, but I hope we will not just go on year in and year out putting up with something that none of us like. Failing something better, I think that the house should support this measure for the relief of parliament from this business which should not be our business at all.

When the house rose at six o'clock we were considering the first item and the minister had made some reply. There were some things in the minister's reply to the speeches made this afternoon to which I take marked exception. During the last session of the house I pointed out that, so far as hospitals in the Dominion of Canada and especially in the province of Ontario were concerned, grants had been given by the province of Ontario-I am not acquainted with the situation in the other provinces- two years before health grants were instituted in this house. When the minister said that we expected so many thousand beds at a certain time owing to these health grants, and that we had achieved so many, I want to call his attention to the fact that a grant of $1,000 per bed is not a solution to the problem of building hospitals even in the province of Ontario where another $1,000 is added to the federal contribution for beds for new cases.
I have in mind a town with which I am well acquainted. It is struggling with the problem of trying to build a hospital at the present time. Let us suppose that the cost of a hospital is approximately $9,000 per bed. Even with the combined grant made by the province of Ontario and the Dominion of Canada that would still leave an amount of $7,000 per bed to be provided by the municipality concerned. It is not so many years ago that the cost of hospital construction was approximately $5,000 per bed. We did not get hospital beds in those days, and I do not think the minister or his department can take all the credit for the fact that we are getting hospital beds now when the cost is really $7,000 or $7,500. In the municipality to which I refer they are raising money by public subscription, and they have had a great deal of difficulty in collecting sufficient money to build a hospital. Across the whole country the need for hospitalization has become a matter of some urgency. I said


this afternoon that it was difficult to obtain help in the home. Trained nurses are not available, so in view of those circumstances we do need hospital beds. While this grant is praiseworthy, and any grant for a purpose like that is praiseworthy, I again call the minister's attention to the fact that the responsibility for the whole scheme of hospitalization in Canada does not rest on his shoulders. The building of hospital beds is not due to the fact that, almost two years ago, this government brought in a program in connection with it.
So far as the health grants are concerned I well recall when they were introduced in May of 1948 by the prime minister. I think every member of this house was glad to see those grants introduced. I never voted for anything with quite as good spirit as I voted for those grants. Ever since that time, when a grant has been made it has been the cause of a rush of publicity. I was amazed last winter when I read in the newspapers that a grant of $1,000 had been made to Kingston penitentiary for the purchase of a machine for the purpose of taking encephalograms. I thought that was taking the thing pretty far. speechtext: Would the minister outline some of the anti-narcotic work carried on by his department, which is so very valuable to the country and particularly to the Pacific coast?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
This division is one of the oldest in the department, in fact it was one of those that were set up under the original department of pensions and soldiers civil reestablishment. It is not only a problem that concentrates in British Columbia, although the natural propinquity of that province to one of the sources of supply does lend itself, in imagination and in reality in part, to the view that the traffic as well as the policing is particularly active in that part of the country. I may say that it is active all over the country.
We have as head of the division a former mounted police officer who is assisted by some others who have had similar experience. In conjunction with the personnel of the department, the doctors and technical men, they carry out the policy, but the actual enforcement and detection is assisted by the very able work of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. My hon. friend knows that prosecutions take place fairly frequently and indicate the firm desirability of making enforcement effective. From the observations and commendations that have been made by the opium committee of the United Nations I think I can say that the enforcement of this particular division is one that comes up to the expectations of those who were signatories to the opium agreement of the United Nations.
I want to take this opportunity to thank the attorneys general of the various provinces for the co-operation of their legal departments in the enforcement of this matter.

The functions of this division are to try to bring about a co-ordination of efforts in the industrial health field both federal and provincial, particularly in connection with coal mines, factories, and the like. We seek to carry out educational and investigational work in conjunction with the provinces in matters relative to the maintenance and improvement of the health of Canada's working population. We provide technical services by the industrial health laboratory in relation to the above. We also have a consulting service that makes contributions not only directly to provincial governments in this field but also to private industries. In other words, we seek on our level to bring about co-ordination of those activities which the industrial divisions of the departments of health in the provinces seek to carry out to improve the working conditions of men and women in our large urban centres, coal mines and the like.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE

Health services-
230. Health insurance studies, $68,241.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I indicated earlier it is not my intention to repeat the speech I made on the first item, but I should like to say enough to get the minister to say something about this whole question of health insurance studies. As the minister knows, I have been asking questions about this item for a good many years. I hope that the questions I have been asking have been helpful, and that they have prodded the department into trying to do a little more in this field. I have yet to be convinced, if I may put it that way, that the department is doing all it should do in what this heading implies, namely, actually studying health insurance for Canada. I wonder whether the name of this vote should not be changed to make it clear that it is being used mainly for the administration of the health grants, which is a later item in the estimates.
As I indicated this afternoon I put some questions on the order paper this year concerning this matter of health insurance studies. One set of questions was answered on March 16, 1950. I gave the information this afternoon as to the failure of the department to spend all of the money voted for that

Supply-Health and Welfare purpose, but in addition to that I asked the following questions appearing on page 827 of Hansard of March 16, 1950:
How much of the time of the persons indicated in the answer to question 3 has been spent on health insurance studies, and what other tasks have these persons performed?
To paraphrase the answer briefly, I was told that no apportionment of the work of the people paid under this vote could be made accurately; that these people were engaged both in health insurance studies and in the administration of the health grants. That information was given on page 832 of Hansard for March 16, 1950, as well as a statement by the former prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, to the effect that work on health grants should be considered as work preparatory to health insurance.
Another question which I asked on that occasion was this:
Is there available any report summarizing the results of health insurance studies made under the items noted above?
"The items noted above" were the votes for health insurance studies spread over a period of four or five years. The answer referred me to the annual reports of the department for various years, and at various pages. I noted particularly a reference to the last annual report for the year ending March 31, 1949, pages 77 to 88. I had looked at this report before and missed that reference, but I was encouraged to look again because pages 77 to 88 inclusive meant a total of 12 pages in which I could read about the work done under health insurance studies. I went back to the annual report for the year ending March 31, 1949, and turned to pages 77 to 88. The main heading on that page in large twenty-four or thirty point type is "Health insurance studies". But when I read the twelve pages I found that the only reference to health insurance studies is set out at the bottom of page 78. I almost missed it but by reading closely I found it. It reads as follows:
Considerable expansion of the health insurance studies directorate occurred following announcement of the national health program. Its activities have been connected mainly with administration of the grant program, although fundamental studies on health insurance and related matters have not been neglected.
That is all there is in those twelve pages to which I was referred that deals directly with health insurance studies. The remainder of that chapter deals with federal health grants.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend permit just one interruption? When I suggested this afternoon that he might want to make his speech on this subject on this item, he thought he had better give it on the general item. I


do not want to quarrel with him for doing it. Let me assure him of this. We are making most careful studies of this whole problem. We are waiting now for the results of the important surveys that are being conducted by every one of the provincial governments. The cost figures that will come out of those surveys are an integral part of anything that might be done. I want to assure my friend that we are making most serious studies. As he knows, we have brought into the department a number of individuals, one of whom has had previous experience in the matter of health insurance with one of the provinces. We are constantly encouraging, through that division and through our research division, a most careful study of this matter.
While my hon. friend may refer to that question and the answer given in the way he has, I am not criticizing that, but in order to expedite this matter I want him to know, and I believe he will accept this, that we are giving this matter the fullest, most scientific consideration any group of people engaged in the public service of this country can give. We are doing that not only on our own but in collaboration with certain provincial bodies, provincial governments, and with some of the personnel of those provincial governments who have had experience. Two officials of the department have gone to the United Kingdom to make careful spot studies for us in connection with certain phases of the problem. I want my hon. friend to know that we are not neglecting this matter. I hope that this intervention will save him much of the energy which he otherwise might have expended.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It is exceedingly difficult to do otherwise than accept the assurance the minister gives, especially when he gives it in that inimitable tone of voice which he has just used. I do say that the kind of assurance he has sought to give me now sounds to me to have a little more substance in it than the assurance given me in previous years. The trouble is I have felt that way every year. There is something in the minister's tone of voice that makes me change my mind. Every year I rise determined to blast the daylights out of the minister for doing nothing about this matter, but then he gets up and tells me in this tone of voice about what is being done and I decide to give him another year. Then, the next year the tone of voice is stepped up a bit, but he tells me-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The same old thing.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
He tells me the same thing that is in the report. It is buried somewhere in the twelve pages that are supposed to be

devoted to this question of health insurance studies. He said the matter is not being neglected, and that is all his department said in its annual report, that fundamental studies on health insurance and related matters have not been neglected. I have to associate with this the fact that the minister said this afternoon, if I understood him correctly, that he is more concerned about getting health services started than he is about health insurance. I want the health services developed too, but I feel that greater priority than has yet been, given should be shown this business of health insurance. No purpose is served by having the finest hospitals and doctors available to our people if our people cannot afford to make use of those services. That is the purpose of health insurance, to distribute the incidence of the cost so that the people who are ill or who need a preventive health service can get it regardless of their financial position.
I do not quite know whether to take the minister's assurance as having more substance than it has had in former years. I suppose I shall have to give him another chance. But I remind him that it took a good many pages in Hansard for the minister to answer the questions that I put on the order paper; six pages, in fact. It took all that space to answer a small question that occupied about two inches in one column. Later on another question produced another long answer, all of which suggests to me that the people who drafted these replies for the minister felt their job was to make it look good, to make it look as though they were doing something in the field of health insurance studies, whether they were or not. As a matter of fact most of the time of the people paid under this grant is being given to an important job, but that job is the administration of the health grants and not to studying health insurance.
I want to see this country reach the point where we have the finest medical and hospital services available, but I want them to be available to our people. I want our people to be able to afford them, and the only way that can be done is by a health insurance program which would cover all the people of the country. One of the advantages of old age pensions being before a committee and therefore not debatable here at the moment, if I may say so, is that the committee is forced to discuss this other question. I think that is good. It means we are giving some priority tonight to the question of health, and I urge the minister to realize that in this field of health it is not just the provision of services that matters but that health insurance is equally important. I am glad we are voting
Supply-Health and Welfare more money for this purpose. I hope when I put questions on the order paper next year or ask questions on the estimates the minister will not have to fall back on the assurance that the matter is not being neglected, but will be able to tell me in concrete terms what has been done.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Could I have the information I
asked for?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The figure is $10,200.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
This afternoon when this
subject of health insurance was being discussed the minister very properly made reference to two sound principles. The first was that, the matter of public health services being within the provincial field, anything done in this connection will have to be done in full co-operation with the provinces. The second was that nothing should be done to interfere with the relationship between doctor and patient, which has something very intimate and confidential about it. In view of the fact that the dominion-provincial conference is to be held in September, may I ask the minister if he has taken any steps as yet to see that the matter of a public health program is placed upon the agenda of that conference?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows from the statement made by the Prime Minister, the provinces were invited to suggest the items to be discussed. So far at least one province has included this item among its suggestions, and I expect that other provinces will do the same. So far as I know there has been no suggestion along that line as yet from the province of Ontario, but the suggestion has been made by at least one province, if not two, so the item certainly will be on the agenda.

Item agreed to.
Health services-
234. Blindness control, $35,320.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Would the minister say exactly what his department is doing in regard to blindness control? I notice that only $6,000 is being provided for professional and special services, and I believe much more work should be done in this connection in Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is touching a point that interests me very greatly. He will remember when I had the privilege of announcing that we would commence paying pensions to the blind at age 21, and we believe every endeavour should be made to see that those in receipt of pensions as well as those who are potential beneficiaries of pensions to the blind are so treated as to remove the necessity for pensions. We have a program

Supply-Health and Welfare with three provinces, and are prepared to enter into arrangements with all provinces, for dealing with people who are blind or going blind, in order to give them the necessary surgical and medical attention to prevent blindness. We have had some results. I know of one case which was brought to me by an hon. gentleman, the late Maurice Hartt. We were able to provide the necessary surgical treatment for this person, who was in receipt of a blind pension, as a result of which his eyesight was restored and he is no longer on the pension rolls.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Do I understand that the only people who can be helped under this item are those in receipt of blind pensions?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is right.	.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What is done for the other people, who are not in receipt of pensions?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is a provincial responsibility, and some of the provinces are doing great work in that regard. This item has to do with people who are in receipt of blind pensions. It does not mean they must be totally blind, but they must have the degree of blindness which entitles them to a pension.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I do not want to hold up the item, but I am interested in this matter. I wonder if some campaign could not be put on to help these people. For instance, a person with too much sugar in his system will go blind. They are the people who get cataracts on their eyes, but that is not widely known. I believe matters like that could be put into the department's monthly bulletins.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Under the health grants we have two projects dealing with this very matter. We have under consideration now a pamphlet that we hope will receive wide circulation and which I know the Canadian National Institute for the Blind will be very interested in seeing.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Then I am just going to pass on a little advice. In the Senate we have Dr. Veniot, who I think knows more about blindness and its cure than almost anyone else in the country.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: He is a very good man.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If the minister would have a conference with him and get his suggestions-

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: We have talked about it many times.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Then I hope you accept his suggestions.
Item agreed to.

Health services-
235. Epidemiology, $35,780.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I should like to feel that I understood something about this item. Will the minister tell us in a word or two what is being done about this? I know what it means now.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If my hon. friend had consulted me instead of the dictionary I might have been able to give him the right answer and save his eyesight. This division was recommended first of all by the dominion council of health, which proposed the setting up of an organization in our department with regard to epidemics and the whole question of epidemiology. We acted upon that suggestion and made arrangements with the Rockefeller foundation, who made a survey of the health department organizations in the country in respect of this matter and then recommended the present set-up, which is essentially one of co-ordination in connection with similar efforts being made in some of the provinces. The functions of the division are to plan, co-ordinate and execute a national epidemiological program in conjunction with divisions or departments of governments, universities and certain organized groups in the dominion. It seeks to study the incidence and spread of disease in order to achieve adequate control methods throughout Canada. It conducts investigations info the control of those diseases which involve more than one province, or which by mutual agreement with the provinces are considered federal rather than provincial, such as plague, shellfish poisoning, and the like.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Does that mean there is a separate scientific department set up and working here in Ottawa doing that sort of thing? While I am on my feet, is any use made of the scientific set-up at the various universities?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Oh, a great deal. As a matter of fact Dr. Peart, the head of the division, is doing some work at Harvard now in connection with a study that was initiated at one of our Canadian universities. He is following up some work there because they have some special equipment.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Does the minister happen to know of any 'tangible result that can be expected, although not overnight? Is there any special tangible result to date?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I cannot say there have been any tangible results. This is a new division. At first we had difficulty getting personnel, but in conjunction with our laboratory of

hygiene they are engaged with the universities and our own laboratory in a series of studies, all of which adds to the totality of knowledge, and results in achievement. But to say that we have there concrete things, no; to say they are exercising supervisory interest and continuing interest in all these matters, certainly yes, and very definitely.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: How many -of the provinces are at work on this?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: We have relations with eight of the provinces. We have theoretical relations with all ten in this field. There are two provinces that are not themselves sufficiently organized to make collaboration completely effective with them at the moment, but that collaboration will be made effective before too many months.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
How old is
this division?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: This particular division goes back about three and a half years in its present form.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: How many provinces had special divisions of this kind before?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I cannot say the exact number. I think there were about three. Dr. Jackson says four. I knew it was about that number.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The minister considered it necessary to have this additional organization in addition to what the provinces were doing?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The provinces themselves were the ones who asked for it. As 1 explained this afternoon, we have a dominion council of health that meets twice a year. The dominion council of health is a body made up of all provincial departments of health and the federal government. They meet in Ottawa. We bring them here and we discuss common matters, namely, those matters on which they can do a better job; those matters where we need not have duplication of effort; those matters where there should be coordination and the like.

Item agreed to.
National health branch-
Health services-
237.	Medical services-Indians and Eskimos, $11,694,839.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I notice that this item is for Indians and Eskimos. Are they on a par to qualify for this assistance? Or am I correct in understanding that a full-blooded Indian to qualify must be a treaty Indian and reside within the boundaries of a reserve?
Supply-Health and Welfare

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The answer is the latter. But I may say that while we have to realize the obligation under our financial commitments there are many areas where it is impossible to distinguish between the two groups.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: It would be helpful to the committee if the minister at the start of our consideration of the medical services for Indians and Eskimos would give us an outline as to what has been accomplished during the past year, particularly in the matter of extension of hospital services, and the reaching out, if I might call it that, of medical services to the Indians in the outlying areas; also what number of Indians have now been X-rayed for tuberculosis, and what was the result of that survey, and what steps have been taken to deal with the Indians who were found to be suffering from that disease.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
As my hon. friend knows, the expenditures in this particular division have increased sixfold in the last six years. The total budget now for Indian medical services is about $11,700,000. Five years ago it was about $2 million. Eight years ago it was under $800,000. With these expenditures we are building up a whole network of hospital institutions across this country for the main purpose of doing our best to stamp out tuberculosis among the Indian and Eskimo population of this country. These hospitals are strategically located all over the country. To them must be added the number of nursing stations which are being built, the number of nurses who are being added to attend these institutions and the number of permanent and part-time doctors all over the country. I may say that the results are certainly most encouraging. To discharge on behalf of the people of this country the accepted responsibility for the health of 130,000 Indians and
8,000	Eskimos, we have a trained staff now of 1,150 in Indian health services. We have several hundred dentists who give part-time service, as well as some who give full-time service, although I must admit that our dental service program in this particular is not as complete as I should like to see it. The reason for that is largely the difficulty of getting dental personnel.
The results of this program of hospitalization enable me to say tonight that our statistics since 1944 show a 40 per cent decline in the tuberculosis mortality rate among Indians. I think that is an achievement of which this whole country should be proud, not an achievement that I am not responsible for; I am not putting it forward on that basis, but one that the director and those under him have to their credit in trying to stamp out this dread disease.
3910	HOUSE OF
Supply-Health and Welfare
There are many areas yet where the job is colossal, but one of the things that I said in this house when I took over this portfolio on the first presentation of my estimates was that one of our objectives was to stamp out this dread disease. I said that we were doing our best to create the services by which this disease could be stamped out. With that in mind we have undertaken an X-ray program, which enables me to say tonight that in 1949, 75 per cent of Canada's entire native population was given a chest X-ray. That is no mean achievment. As a result of these X-rays, not only have we learned the incidence of t.b. but incidentally we have learned the prevalence of other diseases, and of other illnesses in Indians which, but for these X-rays, would not have been detected.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am glad to hear of the improvement which has taken place as far as t.b. is concerned. I wonder whether the minister can tell us what the t.b. rate is at the present time amongst the Indians and what it is amongst the white population?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes, I have that. Tubercular deaths per 100,000 population of Indians-I am giving the figures now for 1948-were 480-1 and 32-4 for the whites. My hon. friend has the figures that I gave last year which show the tremendous improvement. For instance, in 1947 it was 549 for the Indians and 38-2 for the whites.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The last figures the minister has are the rates for 1948? He has not the rates for 1949?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I have some figures, but they are not official yet.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I trust that this improvement between 1947-48 has continued. This rate is still extraordinarily high. I think the minister realizes that, but there is still considerable improvement to take place. There is still a great deal of work to be done along that line.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: There is no doubt about that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I know the director and the people in the Indian health services branch know that, and are working on these problems. To come back to the matter of hospital construction, nursing stations and the like, can the minister tell us what hospitals were constructed or finished last year, and what nursing stations were put up?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The only hospital actually opened last year was at Sioux Lookout, besides about eleven nursing stations.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Do I understand from that that this entire amount of $2,800,000 was spent on the Sioux Lookout hospital and the eleven nursing stations, or was a considerable amount of that on buildings to be completed in the coming year-or what is the situation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What does "yes" mean?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Completed this year.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: What Indian hospitals did this vote cover? What ones are now under construction; and how many, if any, will be completed this year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Norway House, Moose Factory and Hobbema.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Are those hospitals or nursing stations?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Of course additional to this are some hospital residences in remote areas where we have to have hospital residences in order to attract medical personnel. In one place we have a nurses' residence, and two laundry buildings.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: As I understand it, there are two hospitals covered in this vote. They may be completed this year. Then there are residences for medical personnel. Is that the general situation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Three hospitals.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Are there any more nursing stations to be built this year, or is the program for nursing stations now complete?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: No, there are eighteen new ones.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Eighteen more included in this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Are they pretty well scattered over the entire dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes, all across the dominion.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Then my next question concerns personnel. Looking at page 186 of the estimates there would seem to be 88 permanent employees and 1,094 temporary employees. In addition to this there are casual and other assistants amounting to $40,000 last year and $75,000 this year. What is the explanation for this proportion of about twelve to one of temporary as compared with permanent employees? Are a large number of these 1,094 temporaries part-time doctors? If so, how many are part-time doctors, and what are the others who come under that classification?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: In the first place, our quota in the Indian health division is 30 per cent. The hon. member will understand that we have to maintain a balance between permanent and temporary employees.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Quota of what?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Our quota of permanent employees is 30 per cent. The large number

of temporaries is, first of all, due to that circumstance, and to the fact that we have engaged throughout the country a shifting personnel including orderlies, ward aides, men to look after furnaces, men to drive trucks and, as the Minister of Public Works says, charwomen. Then there are a large percentage of Indian personnel whom we seek to encourage.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The minister says the quota of permanent employees is 30 per cent. However, the present quota is down to 8 per cent. That seems to be an extremely small number of people in permanent positions-and I suggest that in most instances having permanent employees tends to give a more efficient service.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: We are working up to it. However, this branch, in the form in which it is, was established only in 1945. There has been a very great acceleration of the Indian health service work. As quickly as we can get it up to permanent status my hon. friend may be sure we will do so.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: To what extent are the Indians in the outlying areas now receiving medical assistance? I am thinking particularly of a group of Indians at Nordegg who have recently signed a treaty in Alber.a. Supply-Health and Welfare
