maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
This is the item under which federal grants for hospital construction are made. I should like to detain the house for a few minutes to discuss this matter, as it is most important to my constituents who are trying to build a new hospital wing. These federal grants have gone a long way toward alleviating the shortage of hospital beds in the nation but we have still a considerable distance to go. In my own home city for instance, some nights there are as many as 150 people who cannot get hospital beds. At times the doctors have to send patients to hotel rooms.
As I say, these federal grants are all to the good and I congratulate the minister on having introduced them. However, there are certain weaknesses in the legislation which

makes it impossible for some municipalities and cities to properly utilize it. We in Moose Jaw want to take advantage of these grants but so far we have not been able to, and there are many other municipalities in the same position. The Auditor General's report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1949, shows that of the $13 million voted by this parliament for hospital construction a total of more than $10 million was allowed to lapse. This must be evidence of some weaknesses in the legislation.
I have had considerable correspondence with hospital authorities, with doctors, and with city councillors in Moose Jaw, and I have been asked to propose to the minister a few changes in the legislation so that more municipalities may take advantage of it.
The first weakness, as I see it, is that these grants are made only for the purpose of providing new beds. They are apparently based on the premise that other facilities are not needed. The shortcomings of this formula are obvious. With modern advances in hospital care, the need for extended facilities and up-to-date equipment has increased enormously.
Today in Canada there are dozens of hospitals which have enough beds but which lack X-ray rooms, operating rooms, diet kitchens and things like that. Unless the federal government is concerned more with quantity than with quality, surely the formula should be revised to take care of the need for these central services. To say that our hospitals can be improved only by the addition of beds, is like saying that improvements in our railroad system should be measured only by the number of box cars we add to it.
Many hospital authorities have asked for such a change. For instance, the Canadian* Hospital Council, which met recently in convention, passed the following resolution:
Be it resolved that the Canadian Hospital Council request the Minister oi National Health and Welfare to extend the scope of hospital construction grants, to cover part of the costs of construction of . . . essential and supporting services, and further be it resolved that construction grants apply to all new constructions . . . where it can be shown that an existent structure is obsolete for efficient patient care.
I ask the minister to consider changing these grants so that these central facilities may be provided as well as new beds.
A second weakness in the legislation, as I understand it, is that it does not include assistance for the construction of nurses' residences. Obviously there is not much use in providing a lot of beds, if you do not have nurses to look after the patients. They might as well stay at home. There have been many requests from responsible authorities to have

assistance for this kind of construction provided. For instance, the Canadian Hospital Council at its last annual meeting asked that the grants cover part of the cost of constructing nurses' residences. The Ontario Hospital Association made the same request, as did the Alberta Hospital Association.
The third weakness of the legislation I believe is the rigidity of the financial clause in order in council P.C. 2060. This reads:
That the estimates provide that the distribution of the amount each province may become entitled to receive shall be on the basis of $1,000 for each active treatment bed or bed equivalent and $1,500 per chronic or convalescent bed as hereinafter defined.
The order in council provides that payment shall be made of the balance required to provide:
an amount up to one-third of the total cost of construction or to provide an amount calculated on the basis set forth in paragraph (a) of this section ($1,000 per active treatment bed or $1,500 per chronic or invalid bed), whichever is the lesser.
Theoretically the present legislation provides that the federal government will grant up to one-third the cost of building a hospital but the experience in most provinces over the past several years is that the federal grant never exceeds 20 per cent; and, as far as university hospitals are concerned, it is sometimes only 10 per cent. Premier Duplessis of Quebec made the following statement on October 15, 1949, as reported in the Quebec Chronicle-Telegram:
The federal contribution represents about one-tenth of the cost of each new hospital bed in this province with the other nine-tenths being paid by cheque and by the institutions interested.
As I see it, this is the result of a formula which is based on a net gain in beds, which certainly is no gauge of the hospital's usefulness or of its cost. It seems to me that the formula would be much more useful if it were to provide that the federal government would match the provincial contribution, whatever the amount might be, for each hospital project.
I think it is obvious, and I think the minister will admit, that while a lot of good has been accomplished, there are nevertheless certain weaknesses to the order in council. I suggest to the minister that while the legislation is before us he should consider amending it. I do not feel it would cost the taxpayers any more money, and it would make the act much more effective.
I have then four recommendations to make to the minister. First of all, I suggest that he permit the grants to be used at least in part for extending laboratories, X-ray, operating room, dietary and other administration facilities. Second, I suggest that he permit the grants to be used when necessary
Supply-Health and Welfare for the establishment of nurses' residences. Third, I suggest that he permit the federal government to pay one-third of the costs of construction, whatever the amount might be, for each hospital project as long as the provincial government recommends it. Fourth, I suggest that the federal government should make loans available to the municipalities at low interest rates to help them finance their share of the cost, and allow them to repay the loans over a period of years.
These are suggestions which would help us in Moose Jaw. I think they would help in many parts of Canada. I wish the minister would tell parliament and the people what he can do in this connection.

As a member of the opposition I must confess to some resentment at the statement made by the minister this afternoon to the effect that members of the opposition are irritated by the accomplishments of his department. I trust that the minister was not entirely serious in making that statement. In so far as I am concerned, I may say that, because of the benefit to the people of Canada as a whole, I would be delighted to acknowledge a brilliant success in the minister's department, but I would want that success to be one of efficiency as well as brilliancy. I would want the department to use every dollar expended to its fullest extent. I think that is the purpose for which we are examining these estimates in detail. We are all gravely concerned about this department. So far as my own riding is concerned, I like to know where this money is being spent, and what results are being obtained. Everything that is spent in the department of welfare reflects itself in municipal costs. Municipal costs in turn reflect themselves in the tax rates which are struck in the municipalities, which in turn become a burden upon the small home owner. After several years' experience in municipal work I have become keenly conscious of the increasing burden which is borne by the small home owners of this country by reason of welfare costs which are paid by municipalities, and which I have always maintained and still maintain should be assumed by some higher levels of government.

Mr. Chairman, I take up the challenge which the minister threw out this afternoon. I should like to make a definite suggestion in connection with this item. I notice that in the details on page 189, at the foot of the page, there is the note "educational and informational publicity", and the amount of the estimate is reduced from $95,000 for last year to $56,500 for this year. From that I would presume that the activities of this department are to be curtailed. I should like to suggest that some of this money be spent in giving advice to at least some of the recipients of family allowances. The suggestion which I have to make is that the department should consider enclosing with the family allowance cheques dietary advice.
I realize there are many people in this country who probably do not need such advice, and who are well informed. But there are a great many others who do need it. Today there are families living in two and three rooms in many municipalities in this country. Under the conditions which prevail in housing, they are living in quarters in which there is no adequate provision for food storage so it is necessary for them to live from hand to mouth. The children come home from school at noon, and the mother sends them out to the corner grocery store. They return with small quantities of food, such as a few slices of cooked meat and even a quarter pound of butter because they cannot store larger quantities. Owing to this situation the money which is going into those homes, ostensibly for the care of those children, for nutrition and so on, is being spent on the most expensive type of food that the homemaker can buy. It is being spent on that food because, in many instances, the mother of the
Supply-Health and Welfare family does not realize there is a better way in which to spend that money.
I believe that the department could serve a useful purpose in ensuring the more efficient use of the moneys which are expended on family allowances if a careful study of this question were made, and if this information were given to the mothers in simple form. There should not be too many suggestions on one sheet, but a simple enclosure with each family allowance cheque suggesting inexpensive meals, and various domestic economies in the purchase of foods and the storage of food which would be practicable in those restricted quarters. As I said before, Mr. Chairman, I am throwing out this suggestion to the minister. I do not want to take up too much time on this particular point, but I think it is worth while for the department to consider some manner, after the exchanges which have taken place here today, of getting the publicity of the department to serve a more useful purpose.
